name: BIY metric bank
design_notes: The bank has one row per measurement a client benchmark can actually run. Public exams (MMLU, BIG-bench, GSM8K, HELM scenarios, Arena Elo) are priors, not metrics. Where Ragas and DeepEval name the same construct, one row is kept and the other name is an alias. Metrics marked avoid_as_primary exist so a selector can refuse BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, fluency, or embedding cosine as the sole quality score. Operational metrics are measured on the same run as quality. Only utility_axis=quality scores enter the 0–1 quality average, and they must already be higher-better. Lower-better risk rates are gates. A client scorecard should contain the always-on operational metrics, one speed metric chosen from the use-case kind, one to five quality metrics, and zero to five risk gates. Document vision is included for pages and scans: character and word error, plus box overlap. Speech, image aesthetics, and caption preference are not. The bank is a library, not a list to run in full.

selection_policy.quality_rule: A metric may enter the quality average Q only when utility_axis is quality and the stored score is higher-better on 0–1. Apply quality_transform before averaging. Do not min-max Q across candidates.
selection_policy.gate_rule: Gates are hard failures. Use them for schema validity, error rate, harmful compliance, confirmed privacy leaks, and latency ceilings the client named. Do not turn every metric into a gate.
selection_policy.judge_rule: Prefer a named deterministic or claim-level metric over a generic judge. Select at most one of rubric_score and g_eval. Add pairwise_vs_baseline only when a baseline completion exists.

categories.name: Accuracy and classification
categories.description: Deterministic correctness against a reference, a label, or a required string.
categories.selector_notes: Prefer these over a judge whenever a gold string, label, or list exists. Lead classification with F1 unless the client named precision or recall.

categories.name: Reasoning
categories.description: Final-answer equivalence, step validity, and stability of quantitative work.
categories.selector_notes: Score the final answer deterministically. Add step correctness only when a person will read the work.

categories.name: Knowledge and factuality
categories.description: Claims checked against a reference answer, a corpus, or a dated key.
categories.selector_notes: If the product must stay inside a retrieved document, use faithfulness instead of a knowledge metric.

categories.name: RAG and grounding
categories.description: Whether the answer is supported by retrieved context, and whether retrieval did its job.
categories.selector_notes: Faithfulness and answer relevancy grade the generator. Context metrics grade retrieval. Do not grade retrieval when context is frozen.

categories.name: Summarization
categories.description: Coverage, coherence, and length of summaries. Consistency with the source is faithfulness.
categories.selector_notes: Do not select ROUGE or BERTScore as the quality metric. Use coverage plus faithfulness.

categories.name: Code
categories.description: Execution against tests, syntax, structural similarity, and static security findings.
categories.selector_notes: Tests outrank every similarity metric. Add the insecure-code rate when generated code can be merged.

categories.name: Conversation
categories.description: Multi-turn relevance, memory, role, topic, and whether the dialogue finished the job.
categories.selector_notes: Lead with conversation completeness when a goal exists. Do not apply single-turn RAG metrics to a whole transcript.

categories.name: Instruction following
categories.description: Verifiable constraints from the prompt, scored strictly or per constraint.
categories.selector_notes: Write deterministic verifiers. A judge is a last resort. JSON schema is not this category.

categories.name: Structured output
categories.description: Parse and schema checks, field values, enums, SQL execution, and non-JSON formats.
categories.selector_notes: Gate on schema validity. Put field accuracy in the quality average. Do not also gate on raw JSON parse when the schema gate exists.

categories.name: Document vision
categories.description: Transcription error on text read from an image, and overlap between predicted and reference regions.
categories.selector_notes: Use character accuracy when a reference transcription exists, and report character and word error beside it. Put bbox_f1 in the quality average and report bbox_iou. Do not apply these to a text-only prompt.

categories.name: Agents and tool use
categories.description: Tool choice, argument match, task success, and trajectory discipline.
categories.selector_notes: Single-step products use tool-call match. Multi-step products with a sandbox use task success. Do not exact-match a trajectory when several paths are legal.

categories.name: Multilinguality
categories.description: Language identification, translation quality, cross-lingual agreement, and locale formatting.
categories.selector_notes: Gate on language match when a locale is required. Rank translation with COMET, not BLEU.

categories.name: Safety
categories.description: Harmful compliance, over-refusal, toxicity, injection, and client policy.
categories.selector_notes: These are gates, not quality-average terms. Always pair harmful compliance with over-refusal on user-facing assistants.

categories.name: Bias and fairness
categories.description: Stereotype-aligned choices, counterfactual invariance, and subgroup gaps.
categories.selector_notes: Do not infer sensitive attributes. Use only labels the client is allowed to have, or a reviewed benchmark set.

categories.name: Privacy
categories.description: Personal data, secrets, unnecessary echo, and verbatim regurgitation of a licensed corpus.
categories.selector_notes: Gate secret leakage and confirmed PII leakage for any workflow that sees customer data.

categories.name: Robustness
categories.description: Stability under paraphrase, typos, negation, option order, long context, and user pressure.
categories.selector_notes: Add long-context accuracy when production prompts are long. Do not replace the client's task with a public needle test.

categories.name: Calibration and hallucination
categories.description: Unsupported outputs, confidence versus accuracy, and selective prediction.
categories.selector_notes: Hallucination rate is a gate. Faithfulness is the quality term. ECE needs a real confidence, not a made-up one.

categories.name: Efficiency
categories.description: Latency, decode speed, throughput, and cold start, measured on the same run as quality.
categories.selector_notes: Pick one primary speed metric from the kind: TTFT for chat, end-to-end for sync extraction and classification, task time for agents, none for batch.

categories.name: Cost
categories.description: Dollars per case and per success, token volumes, cache, and a self-host estimate.
categories.selector_notes: Always record cost per case, cost per success, and output tokens. Rank on cost per success.

categories.name: Reliability
categories.description: Errors, truncation, throttling, flip rate, and pass^k.
categories.selector_notes: Always gate on error rate and watch truncation. Add pass^k for agents. Do not call throttling latency.

categories.name: Business and UX
categories.description: Brand voice, human acceptance, containment, satisfaction, and reading level.
categories.selector_notes: Use these when the signal exists in logs or a brand guide. Do not invent CSAT with a judge.

categories.name: Judging methods
categories.description: Generic instruments for criteria that do not have a named metric.
categories.selector_notes: Select at most one of rubric score and G-Eval. Add pairwise versus baseline only when a baseline model is in the run.

priors.name: MMLU and MMLU-Pro
priors.useful_as: A weak prior that a model stored textbook facts.
priors.do_not_use_as: A substitute for the client's domain questions, which have their own distribution and their own wrong answers.
priors.citation: Hendrycks et al., 2020. MMLU-Pro is the harder follow-up.

priors.name: BIG-bench and BIG-bench Hard
priors.what_it_measures: A wide scatter of tasks beyond a single exam, with BBH focusing on items where models once failed.
priors.useful_as: Evidence that a single accuracy number is not a model identity. The suite is a collection, not a client metric.
priors.do_not_use_as: A checklist to run for a customer. Most tasks are not their task.
priors.citation: Srivastava et al., 2022. Suzgun et al., 2022 for BBH.

priors.name: HELM
priors.what_it_measures: Accuracy together with calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency on shared scenarios.
priors.useful_as: The argument for this bank: do not ship a leaderboard that only has accuracy, and do not use a win rate that depends on who else was in the set.
priors.do_not_use_as: A living score to import. HELM's own scenarios are not the client's scenarios. The project has also been described as in maintenance rather than as a product API.
priors.citation: Liang et al., 2022, Holistic Evaluation of Language Models.

priors.name: GSM8K and MATH
priors.useful_as: A prior for arithmetic and symbolic work. The scoring idea, equivalence of the final answer, is in this bank as math_equivalence.
priors.do_not_use_as: Proof a model can compute the client's invoices or doses.
priors.citation: Cobbe et al., 2021. Hendrycks et al., 2021.

priors.name: GPQA
priors.what_it_measures: Graduate-level science questions written to resist shallow search.
priors.useful_as: A prior for hard technical knowledge, not for a support bot.
priors.do_not_use_as: A substitute for the client's own technical questions.

priors.name: IFEval and IFBench
priors.what_it_measures: Verifiable constraints, strictly and loosely, at prompt level and instruction level.
priors.useful_as: The verifier design this bank copies. IFBench is the less saturated follow-up the existing catalogue names.
priors.do_not_use_as: The client's constraint list. Frontier models saturate public IFEval. Run the client's rules.
priors.citation: Zhou et al., 2023. IFBench, Allen Institute for AI.

priors.name: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard
priors.what_it_measures: AST match, executable match, irrelevance, and multi-turn state on function calling.
priors.useful_as: The single-step tool metrics in this bank, and a reminder that the same weights differ by provider.
priors.do_not_use_as: A claim about the client's APIs. Their schemas and side effects are different.
priors.citation: Patil, Mao, Yan, Ji, Suresh, Stoica, Gonzalez. BFCL.

priors.name: τ-bench
priors.what_it_measures: Tool-using agents in a simulated customer workflow, with pass^k for reliability.
priors.useful_as: The definition of task success and pass^k when a sandbox exists.
priors.do_not_use_as: A score for an agent whose tools and policy you have not encoded.

priors.name: SWE-bench
priors.what_it_measures: Whether a patch resolves a real repository issue without breaking existing tests.
priors.useful_as: The patch-resolve metric, when the client has repos and tests.
priors.do_not_use_as: A ranking for a unit-level code assistant. HumanEval-style pass@k is the closer prior, and it is still not their tests.
priors.citation: Jimenez et al., 2024. Chen et al., 2021 for HumanEval pass@k.

priors.name: RULER and needle tests
priors.what_it_measures: Whether a claimed context window still works, including retrieval at positions inside the window.
priors.useful_as: A warning that advertised context length is not effective context. The catalogue lists a RULER subset as an optional prior.
priors.do_not_use_as: The long-context score for a client. Run their task at their length.
priors.citation: Hsieh et al., 2024. Liu et al., 2023 for lost-in-the-middle.

priors.name: JSONSchemaBench
priors.what_it_measures: Schema-constrained generation across a range of schemas.
priors.useful_as: Evidence that schema validity is a real, model-and-provider-dependent failure. The catalogue lists a subset as an optional prior.
priors.do_not_use_as: A substitute for validating the client's own schema.

priors.name: Ragas, DeepEval, and TruLens
priors.what_it_measures: Faithfulness, relevancy, context precision and recall, plus agent and safety checks in DeepEval.
priors.useful_as: The RAG and agent metric definitions this bank canonicalizes. Where two libraries name one construct, the bank keeps one row and lists the other as an alias.
priors.do_not_use_as: A requirement to depend on those packages. The formulas are what matter.
priors.citation: Ragas. DeepEval, Confident AI. TruLens RAG triad.

priors.name: SimpleQA, FActScore, and FACTS Grounding
priors.what_it_measures: Short-form factuality with abstention, atomic-fact precision against a source, and grounding.
priors.useful_as: The knowledge metrics in this bank. FACTS Grounding is a prior for the same construct as faithfulness.
priors.do_not_use_as: A general knowledge leaderboard for a private corpus.
priors.citation: Wei et al., 2024. Min et al., 2023. Google FACTS Grounding.

priors.name: BBQ, RealToxicityPrompts, XSTest, HarmBench
priors.what_it_measures: Ambiguous-context bias, toxicity prompts, over-refusal on benign prompts, and compliance on disallowed prompts.
priors.useful_as: The shapes of the safety and bias metrics. Sets must be reviewed and policy-aligned. This bank does not ship attack content.
priors.do_not_use_as: Permission to generate new jailbreaks inside a client benchmark.
priors.citation: Parrish et al., 2022. Gehman et al., 2020. Röttger et al., 2024. Mazeika et al., HarmBench.

priors.name: LMSYS Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval
priors.what_it_measures: Human or judge preference, with Elo or Bradley-Terry, plus length and style controls.
priors.useful_as: How to run a pairwise comparison against a fixed baseline, and why uncorrected win rates follow length.
priors.do_not_use_as: The quality of a structured extractor. Crowdsourced chat preference is a different product.
priors.citation: Zheng et al., 2023, MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate.

priors.name: Artificial Analysis
priors.what_it_measures: Independent latency, throughput, price, and a composite intelligence index by model and provider.
priors.useful_as: A prior and a vocabulary for TTFT, output speed, and price. The catalogue says to pull the index, not to re-run it as the client's quality.
priors.do_not_use_as: The client's quality number. Their prompts, length mix, and region differ.

priors.name: OpenAI Evals
priors.what_it_measures: A registry of exact match, includes, fuzzy match, and model-graded checks.
priors.useful_as: The idea of small deterministic assertions, which this bank keeps as contains, regex, and exact match.
priors.do_not_use_as: A maintained metric library. The registry is not where new client metrics should come from.

metrics.name: Classification accuracy
metrics.description: Share of items whose predicted label equals the gold label. It is the headline number for balanced routing and intent tasks, and it hides failure on rare classes, which is why imbalanced tasks should lead with classification_f1 or precision and recall.
metrics.measures: Top-1 label correctness against a gold label set.

signals: The output is one label from a known set
Classes are roughly balanced, or accuracy is only a secondary number
Gold labels exist in fixtures, traces, or a reviewed sample

when_not_to_use: The positive class is rare. A model that always predicts the majority class looks accurate. Use classification_f1, precision, and recall.
Labels are free text with no canonical set. Map them to an enum first or use a rubric.

required_inputs.notes: Parse the label from JSON or the raw string before scoring. Config lists the allowed labels.

computation.formula: accuracy = (1/n) * count(pred_i == gold_i)
procedure: Parse a single label from the output.
Treat unparseable output as incorrect, and also count it in format_valid or json_schema_valid.
Report overall accuracy and a confusion matrix. Do not stop at the single number when classes differ in cost.

interpretation.meaning: Every item received its gold label.
Compare with the majority-class baseline before celebrating a high score.
No item matched. Check label parsing before comparing models.

score.aggregation: Micro accuracy over items. Also report per-class recall.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap. The cost is the labeled set, not the arithmetic.

limitations: Accuracy ignores the cost of false positives versus false negatives.
A changing label inventory across candidates makes the number incomparable. Freeze the label set.

metrics.name: Classification F1
metrics.description: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is the default single quality number for intent and routing tasks because it falls when the model buys recall by flooding false positives, or the reverse. The catalogue's default for classification.
metrics.measures: Balance of precision and recall on the label set, under a stated average.

signals: The use case kind is classification
Labels are a closed set and gold labels exist
Classes are imbalanced or the client did not name precision versus recall

when_not_to_use: The business has an explicit precision or recall floor. F1 can look fine while that floor fails. Gate on the floor and still report F1.
Labels are multi-label sets of entities rather than one class. Use set_f1.

required_inputs.notes: Config average is macro by default, matching the catalogue note macro|micro. Macro does not let the majority class dominate.

computation.formula: F1 = 2PR / (P+R). Macro F1 averages per-class F1. Micro F1 pools TP, FP, and FN across classes.
procedure: Parse labels and build the confusion matrix.
Compute the configured F1.
Always attach the confusion matrix so a single F1 is explainable.

interpretation.meaning: Perfect precision and recall on the averaged classes.
Strong for many routing tasks. Compare with the majority and keyword baselines.
Precision or recall is zero for the averaged classes.

score.aggregation: One F1 per candidate under a frozen average. Do not compare macro against micro.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap. Prefer this over accuracy as the number that enters Q for classification.

limitations: Macro F1 treats each class as equal. Switch to micro or weighted only with a written reason.
F1 assumes the label inventory is the same for every candidate.

metrics.name: Classification precision
metrics.description: Of the items the model assigned to a class, the share that truly belong there. Pick this when a false positive is the expensive mistake, as in fraud flags, spam holds, or alarming a clinician.
metrics.measures: How rarely the model raises a false alarm for the classes you configure.

signals: Acting on the label is costly or user-visible
False positives create manual review or customer harm
The product owner names precision, false alarms, or positive predictive value

when_not_to_use: Missing a case is the expensive error, as in adverse-event screening. Lead with classification_recall and treat precision as the trade-off.
Every class matters equally and the set is balanced. classification_f1 is the single number. Still keep precision in the drill-down.

required_inputs.notes: Config selects the positive labels and the average: binary, macro, or micro.

computation.formula: precision = TP / (TP + FP), per class. Macro precision is the unweighted mean across classes. Undefined classes with no predicted positives are skipped and reported as such.
procedure: Build the confusion matrix on parsed labels.
Compute precision for the configured positive classes.
Publish the average the client asked for and the per-class values beside it.

interpretation.meaning: Every positive prediction was correct. Recall may still be poor.
Often the review-cost target for a human-in-the-loop flag.
No positive prediction was correct, or the metric was undefined and coerced only if you explicitly configured that.

score.aggregation: The configured average over classes, never a silent micro/macro swap.
score.suggested_gate: >= a client-set floor when false alarms have a hard cost.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap once labels exist.

limitations: Precision with very few predicted positives is noisy. Report the support.
Macro precision treats a tiny class like a huge one. Confirm that is the business intent.

metrics.name: Classification recall
metrics.description: Of the items that truly belong to a class, the share the model found. Pick this when a miss is the expensive mistake, as in safety escalations, claim types that must not be dropped, or adverse-event screening.
metrics.measures: Coverage of the gold positive items, also called sensitivity or true positive rate.

use_cases: support intents that must always route to a human
signals: Missing a class has a compliance or safety cost
The client says recall, sensitivity, or catch rate
A rare class is the one the product exists to find

when_not_to_use: Extra flags are the problem and misses are cheap. Lead with precision.
You only have predicted labels and no gold. Recall is undefined.

required_inputs.notes: Requires gold labels. Config selects positive labels and the average.

computation.formula: recall = TP / (TP + FN). Macro recall averages per-class recall without weighting by support.
procedure: Build the confusion matrix.
Compute recall for each configured class.
Report support so a perfect score on three examples is not read as a gate.

interpretation.meaning: Every gold positive was found. Precision may still be poor.
A typical floor when a miss is a compliance event. Confirm with the client.
No gold positive was found.

score.aggregation: Configured class average, with support reported.
score.suggested_gate: >= a client-set floor for classes whose misses are unacceptable.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap once labels exist.

limitations: Recall can be gamed by predicting the positive class always. Read it next to precision.
Label noise on the rare class moves the score more than model changes do.

metrics.name: Contains all
metrics.description: The output contains every required string. It is a deterministic gate for must-mention facts, required phrases, and keywords the product promised to include.
metrics.measures: Presence of a configured list of substrings or normalized phrases.

use_cases: answers that must name a specific policy id
signals: The prompt lists phrases that must appear
A compliance sentence is mandatory
Tests assert that the output includes certain strings

when_not_to_use: The required content can be paraphrased. Substring checks then false-fail. Use a constraint judged for meaning, or list aliases in config.
You are trying to ban phrases. That is contains_none.

required_inputs.notes: Config strings[] is the required list. Matching is case-insensitive by default and can take aliases per item.

computation.formula: score = 1 if every required item has a match in the output, else 0. The diagnostic rate is matched_items / required_items.
procedure: Normalize the output and each required string.
Score the case 1 only when all items match.
Report the fractional coverage as a diagnostic so one missing disclaimer is visible.

interpretation.meaning: Every required string was present.
At least one required string was missing.

score.aggregation: Mean of per-case pass bits. Also report mean item coverage.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 when a missing phrase is a compliance failure.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap enough to use as a gate on every run.

limitations: Substring presence is not understanding. A negated disclaimer can still match.
Translations fail the check unless each locale has its own string list.

metrics.name: Contains none
metrics.description: The output contains none of a banned list. Use it for competitor names, forbidden claims, and phrases legal has already enumerated. It is a gate, not a general safety evaluation.
metrics.measures: Absence of configured banned substrings.

use_cases: phrases that must not appear in a regulated reply
signals: Brand or legal guidance lists forbidden words
The prompt says never mention X
Tests assert that certain strings are absent

when_not_to_use: The harm is not a known phrase. Toxicity, medical advice, or jailbreaks need safety metrics, not a word list.
The banned string is a substring of an allowed word. Tune the matcher to tokens or you will false-fail.

required_inputs.notes: Config strings[] is the ban list. This does not require a judge.

computation.formula: score = 1 if no banned item matches, else 0.
procedure: Normalize the output.
Search each banned pattern.
Fail the case on the first hit and record which pattern fired.

interpretation.meaning: No banned string appeared.
At least one banned string appeared.

score.aggregation: Mean of per-case passes. A gate usually requires a very high mean.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 for explicit legal or brand bans.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap gate. Do not confuse it with a safety eval.

limitations: Lists do not catch paraphrased violations.
A ban on a common token creates false failures. Review hits.

metrics.name: Exact match
metrics.description: The normalized prediction equals the reference string. This is the right score when the task has one canonical answer, as in short extraction, closed labels, and some QA sets after SQuAD-style normalization.
metrics.measures: Whether the output is the reference, not whether it is merely similar or fluent.

signals: A fixture or gold string exists for the field
Downstream code compares the output with == after light cleanup
The answer is a name, id, date, or other short canonical string

when_not_to_use: Several phrasings are acceptable. Exact match then punishes correct paraphrases. Use token_f1 or a rubric.
The output is a paragraph, summary, or chat reply. Character identity is not quality.

required_inputs.notes: Config normalize defaults to true: casefold, strip punctuation and articles, collapse whitespace.

computation.formula: EM = 1 if norm(prediction) == norm(reference) else 0. With multiple references, take the max.
procedure: Apply the normalizer unless config.normalize is false.
Compare to each reference and keep the best match.
Aggregate the mean of case scores. Report the unnormalized rate beside it when formatting matters.

interpretation.meaning: Every case matched a reference after the configured normalization.
A reasonable gate for short canonical fields such as currency codes.
No case matched. Check the normalizer before blaming the model.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 only when the field truly has one spelling and downstream code requires it.

cost_effort.driver: String compare on data you already stored.
cost_effort.notes: Negligible next to the model call. The expensive part is writing references.

limitations: A single gold string hides legitimate variants. Collect aliases or the score understates quality.
Normalization can hide real errors, such as dropped punctuation in legal citations. Turn it off for those fields.

metrics.name: Matthews correlation coefficient
metrics.description: A correlation between predicted and gold labels that uses all four cells of the confusion matrix. It stays informative when classes are heavily imbalanced, where accuracy and sometimes F1 flatter a majority classifier.
metrics.measures: Agreement with gold labels corrected for chance in the binary and multiclass generalizations.

use_cases: any classifier you might otherwise rank by accuracy
signals: Positive labels are a small fraction of the set
Stakeholders have been misled by accuracy on this task before
You want one imbalance-aware number next to F1

when_not_to_use: The client needs a probability they can explain as precision or recall. MCC is harder to narrate. Lead with those and keep MCC as support.
You have fewer than a few dozen positives. The coefficient jumps around.

required_inputs.notes: Works for binary and multiclass labels. Not a probability calibration metric.

computation.formula: Binary MCC = (TP*TN - FP*FN) / sqrt((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)). Multiclass uses the Gorodkin generalization. Range is -1 to 1.
procedure: Build the confusion matrix from parsed labels.
Compute MCC. Map it into Q as (MCC + 1) / 2 only if you intentionally put it on the quality axis.
This bank keeps MCC as a diagnostic correlation and does not fold it into Q.

interpretation.meaning: Perfect prediction.
No better than a chance association given the class margins.
Perfectly wrong.

score.aggregation: One coefficient per candidate on the full labeled set.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap diagnostic next to F1.

limitations: Stakeholders rarely know the scale. Do not put MCC alone on a recommendation card.
The quality axis of BIY expects 0–1 higher-better scores. Leave MCC off Q.

metrics.name: Regex match
metrics.description: The output matches a regular expression. Use it for formats that are awkward in JSON Schema, such as ticket ids, citation styles, or 'exactly one URL'. Prefer json_schema_valid when the whole payload is structured.
metrics.measures: Whether the output, or a configured capture, matches a pattern.

signals: The required shape is a pattern rather than a schema
Existing tests use a regex on the model output
JSON schema would be a poor fit for one field inside free text

when_not_to_use: The payload is JSON with types and required fields. A regex on JSON is brittle. Use json_schema_valid.
The pattern encodes a legal or safety policy. Patterns rot and miss paraphrases.

required_inputs.notes: Config pattern is required. Config group can score a captured group against a reference.

computation.formula: score = 1 if re.search(pattern, output) succeeds under the configured flags, else 0.
procedure: Compile the pattern once and reject patterns that are unbounded or catastrophic.
Search each output.
Average the passes. Store the pattern version with the run.

interpretation.meaning: Every output matched the pattern.
No output matched. Confirm the pattern before comparing models.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 when downstream parsing depends on the pattern.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap. Review the pattern for catastrophic backtracking before running it on model output.

limitations: Regular expressions are a poor substitute for a grammar or a schema.
A pattern that passes the empty string will flatter refusals and truncations.

metrics.name: Semantic similarity
metrics.description: Cosine similarity between embeddings of the prediction and the reference. It detects paraphrase where token overlap fails, and it is not a measure of factual correctness. The selector should refuse it as the only quality metric.
metrics.measures: How close the output sits to the reference in an embedding space.

use_cases: a secondary signal next to a real correctness metric
signals: A reference answer exists and many wordings are acceptable
Someone asks for BERTScore or cosine similarity by name
You are diffing a new model against last month's outputs

when_not_to_use: You need to know whether facts are right. Similar embeddings can share topic and still contradict the reference.
There is no reference. Embedding the output against nothing is undefined. Use a rubric or answer_relevancy.

required_inputs.notes: Pin the embedding model. Scores are not comparable across embedding families.

computation.formula: score = max(0, cos(E(pred), E(ref))). Negative cosines are clipped to 0 so the range stays 0–1.
procedure: Embed the prediction and the reference with the pinned model.
Take cosine similarity and clip negatives to 0.
Average over cases. Do not min-max the scores across candidate models.
implementations: BERTScore is the token-level cousin, see bertscore_f1

interpretation.meaning: Typical of a close paraphrase with a strong English embedding. Calibrate on your own pairs.
Same neighborhood of meaning. Not evidence the answer is correct.
Orthogonal or opposed in the embedding space.

cost_effort.driver: One embedding pass over predictions and references.
cost_effort.notes: Much cheaper than an LLM judge. Still the wrong primary metric for facts.

limitations: The number inherits the embedding model's biases and language coverage.
High similarity does not imply entailment. Pair with faithfulness or factual_correctness.

metrics.name: Set F1
metrics.description: Precision and recall over a set of extracted values, ignoring order. Use it when the model must return a list of entities, codes, or citations and extra or missing members both matter.
metrics.measures: Overlap between the predicted set and the gold set.

signals: The schema field is an array
Order of elements is not meaningful
Both missed and invented elements are errors

when_not_to_use: Order matters, as in a ranked list or a procedure. Use a rank-aware metric or exact_match on the sequence.
There is a single label. classification_f1 is clearer.

required_inputs.notes: Config supplies the field path and a per-element normalizer. Matching can be exact or numeric-tolerance.

computation.formula: P = |pred ∩ gold| / |pred|, R = |pred ∩ gold| / |gold|, F1 = 2PR / (P+R). Empty gold and empty pred score 1. Empty gold and non-empty pred score 0.

Normalize elements and compute set overlap.
Average F1 over cases. Also report mean precision and recall.

Most members overlap. Inspect whether errors are misses or inventions.
No overlap, or the model invented members when the gold set was empty.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap. Parsing failures should be scored as empty predictions and also counted in json_valid.

limitations: Near-duplicate strings count as total misses unless the normalizer merges them.
A huge predicted set can still show decent recall. Read precision with the F1.

metrics.name: Token F1
metrics.description: Bag-of-tokens precision and recall between the prediction and the reference, combined as an F1. It gives partial credit for short answers that overlap the gold text without being identical, which is the SQuAD companion to exact match.
metrics.measures: Lexical overlap with the reference answer, not semantic correctness or groundedness.

use_cases: answers with a few acceptable extra words
signals: References are short phrases rather than full essays
A correct answer may include the gold span plus a few function words
You want a deterministic score and have gold text

when_not_to_use: Paraphrases are the point of the task. Token overlap then misses correct answers. Use factual_correctness or a rubric.
You are scoring summaries or chat. ROUGE-like overlap does not track what readers prefer.

computation.formula: P = |pred ∩ gold| / |pred|, R = |pred ∩ gold| / |gold|, F1 = 2PR / (P+R). Max over references. Tokens are whitespace tokens after normalization.

Count multiset overlap of tokens.

No shared tokens with the reference.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap enough to run on every case beside exact_match.

limitations: Word order is ignored, so a reversed relation can still score well.
Morphology and synonyms count as misses. Do not use the score as a paraphrase metric.

metrics.name: Agent task success
metrics.description: The task ends in the correct world state and the user-visible outcome contains the required facts. This is the τ-bench reward: the database write state matches and the replies include the required information. Prefer it to step-by-step call matching whenever more than one trajectory can be correct.
metrics.measures: Whether the episode achieved the goal, independent of the exact path.

signals: The agent takes several steps
More than one tool sequence can be correct
A sandbox exposes final state

when_not_to_use: You only have a single expected call and no environment. tool_call_correct is the honest metric. Do not simulate a state you do not have.
Success is a subjective conversation with no state. conversation_completeness is the analogue.

required_inputs.notes: The harness resets state, runs the episode, and diffs the result. Required substrings in the reply are part of the τ-bench output reward. The industry list uses retail as the stand-in for commerce tasks.

computation.formula: success = 1 if state_match AND output_match else 0. Run-level pass@1 is the mean. Reliability across repeats is pass_hat_k.
procedure: Reset the sandbox to the task's start state.
Run the agent, recording tool calls and replies.
Compare the final state to gold and check required reply facts. Exclude harness crashes.
implementations: SWE-bench is the code special case patch_resolve_rate

interpretation.meaning: Every task ended in the correct state with the required reply.

No task succeeded.

score.aggregation: Mean over tasks. Publish the state-only and reply-only rates too.

cost_effort.driver: Full episodes with tool execution and, often, a user simulator.
cost_effort.notes: The expensive agent metric. Use single-step tool metrics for the hackathon path, and this when a harness exists.

limitations: The reward can miss policy violations that still land in the right state, such as skipping a required confirmation. Add policy checks if that matters.
User simulators change the score. Pin them.

metrics.name: Goal accuracy
metrics.description: A judge scores whether the agent's final answer meets the user's stated goal, using the trace as evidence. Ragas agent goal accuracy has a reference mode and a reference-free mode. Prefer agent_task_success when state is checkable. Use this when the outcome is a recommendation or a text result rather than a database write.
metrics.measures: Judged achievement of the user goal at the end of the trace.

use_cases: shopping assistants without a single database state
signals: The agent uses tools but the deliverable is an answer
There is no deterministic end state
A reference outcome or a written goal exists

when_not_to_use: The end state is checkable. A judge will be noisier and more expensive than agent_task_success.
Reference-free mode would let the judge decide the goal from the agent's own summary. Do not use that mode for ranking.

required_inputs.notes: Provide the goal in labels. Reference mode compares to an expected outcome. The judge must see the trace so it cannot reward a confident unsupported answer.

computation.formula: goal_accuracy = episodes the judge marks as goal-met / episodes.
procedure: Pass the goal, the trace, and the final answer.
Require a binary met or not met, plus a reason.
Audit a sample against a human, because this is a judge metric standing in for state.

interpretation.meaning: The judge found every goal met.
Most goals met. Read the misses before treating the judge as a launch gate.
No goal was met according to the judge.

cost_effort.driver: One judge call per episode with the trace in context.
cost_effort.notes: Cheaper than a full sandbox only if you already have the traces. Still audit it.

limitations: Judges are impressed by long traces and citations. Require the trace and a written goal.
Reference-free scoring is too circular for a model recommendation.

metrics.name: Hallucinated-tool rate
metrics.description: The share of cases where the model calls a tool name that was not in the provided tool list. Lower is better. This is a schema failure distinct from choosing the wrong real tool. Providers differ on how often the same weights do this.
metrics.measures: How often the model calls a tool name that was not offered.

use_cases: agents with a changing tool list
signals: Tool names are constrained by the request
Logs contain calls to tools that do not exist
You compare providers serving the same weights

when_not_to_use: The product allows the model to propose new tools. Then an unknown name is not a hallucination.
As a quality term in Q next to schema validity. Use it as a gate or a diagnostic.

required_inputs.notes: Compare called names to the request's tool list, case-sensitively, unless the provider is case-insensitive and production matches that.

computation.formula: rate = cases with any call whose name is not in the allow-list / cases. Lower is better.
procedure: Parse called names.
Flag names absent from the request.
Report the rate and the most common invented names.

interpretation.meaning: No invented tool names.
Occasional invented names. Too many for unattended execution.
Every case invented a tool name.

score.suggested_gate: <= 0.01 for unattended tool execution.

cost_effort.notes: Negligible next to the model call. No judge and no extra request.

limitations: A right tool under a slightly wrong name fails, which is what you want for execution and harsh for a human-in-the-loop UI.
Provider repair may hide the raw hallucination. Score the pre-repair call when you can.
provenance: Provider tool-call fidelity, including K2 vendor comparisons

metrics.name: Irrelevance abstention
metrics.description: On requests where no available tool applies, the model does not call one. BFCL's irrelevance category is this metric. Calling a vaguely related tool is a common and expensive failure. This is not unknown_abstention, which is about missing facts in text.
metrics.measures: Correct refusal to call a tool when none applies.

use_cases: assistants with a narrow tool belt
signals: Some user requests are outside the tools
False tool calls hit real APIs
The tool list is smaller than the things users ask

when_not_to_use: Every request in the set should call a tool. Abstention is then a failure, measured by tool_choice_correct.
The model should answer in text from knowledge. You may still want no tool call, but grade the text with a QA metric too.

required_inputs.notes: The label is no_call. Any tool call fails the case. Text refusals and plain answers both count as abstention.

computation.formula: abstention = no_call_predictions / no_call_cases.
procedure: Restrict scoring to the irrelevance slice.
Fail the case if any tool call was emitted.
Report this slice separately from the in-scope tool accuracy.

interpretation.meaning: The model never called a tool on irrelevant requests.
Most irrelevant requests are refused. The misses are real API calls.
Every irrelevant request produced a call.

score.aggregation: Mean over the irrelevance slice only.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.95 when false calls have a side effect.

cost_effort.driver: A check that the tool-call list is empty.
cost_effort.notes: Free. The cost is labeling the slice.

limitations: A model that never calls tools scores perfectly here and fails every real request. Always publish the in-scope accuracy beside it.
Borderline requests make the label noisy. Write the decision rule.

metrics.name: Plan adherence
metrics.description: When the agent writes a plan and then acts, the share of actions that the plan authorized, in an acceptable order. DeepEval's plan adherence is this metric. It catches agents that announce a safe plan and then do something else.
metrics.measures: Consistency between the stated plan and the subsequent actions.

use_cases: agents that show a plan to a user before acting
signals: The product asks the model to plan, then execute
A human approves the plan
Deviating from the approved plan is an incident

when_not_to_use: The agent does not expose a plan. Do not require one only to score it.
The plan is allowed to change after a tool error. Score the updated plan, or you will punish recovery. See tool_error_recovery.

required_inputs.notes: Prefer a structured plan with step ids. A judge is only needed to align free-text steps with tool calls.

computation.formula: adherence = actions consistent with the plan / actions. An action that the plan did not mention fails.
procedure: Parse the plan the user would have seen.
Align each tool call to a plan step.
Score the fraction of calls that were planned, and flag unordered violations if order was required.

interpretation.meaning: Every action was in the plan.
Most actions were planned. The extras need review if a human approved the plan.
Actions did not follow the plan.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.95 when a human approved the plan before execution.

cost_effort.driver: Alignment of steps to calls, cheap if both are structured.
cost_effort.notes: Keep plans structured so this stays deterministic.

limitations: An agent can adhere to a bad plan. Plan quality is a different judgment and is easy to over-score. Prefer task success for 'was the plan good'.
Recovering from a tool error often requires an unplanned step. Allow a replanning event.

metrics.name: Step efficiency
metrics.description: A successful episode is penalized for taking more tool calls than necessary. DeepEval's step efficiency and a simple gold-length ratio are the construct. An agent that wanders and still succeeds should not tie one that succeeds directly, because wandering costs money and error risk.
metrics.measures: How economically a successful agent used steps.

signals: Tool calls cost money or latency
Successful runs vary widely in length
You have a minimum step count or can see pointless repeats

when_not_to_use: Tasks are not succeeding. Efficiency of a failing agent is not a quality win. Gate on success first.
There is no notion of an extra step. Do not punish a longer path that the policy required.

required_inputs.notes: Config min_steps is the shortest known successful trajectory, or a judge labels wasted steps. Prefer the deterministic ratio when min_steps is known.

computation.formula: If the task failed, score 0. If it succeeded, score min(1, min_steps / actual_steps). actual_steps below min_steps still scores 1 only when success is true.
procedure: Score task success first.
Count tool calls, not tokens.
Apply the ratio on successes and zero on failures.

interpretation.meaning: The task succeeded in no more than the minimum steps.
Success took about twice the necessary calls.
The task failed, or the step count was pathological under your cap.

cost_effort.notes: Free given traces and a min-step annotation. A judge that hunts for wasted steps is the expensive variant. Do not use it by default.

limitations: A wrong min_steps punishes a legitimate path. Set the minimum from the policy, not from the shortest lucky sample.
Zeroing failures makes this correlated with task success. Do not also weight success at full strength without noticing the double count.

metrics.name: Tool-argument schema validity
metrics.description: The share of tool calls whose arguments validate against the tool's JSON Schema. This is the agent form of json_schema_valid. The catalogue's default agent gate is json_valid on tool arguments. Prefer this stricter check when a schema exists, and keep json_valid only if the tool has no schema.
metrics.measures: Whether tool-call arguments validate against the tool's schema.

use_cases: any tool call that production will execute
signals: Tools declare a JSON Schema
Invalid arguments cause 4xx errors or wrong actions
The kind is agent

when_not_to_use: You also plan to put json_schema_valid on the same arguments. They are the same gate. Pick this id for tools.
The schema is empty or additionalProperties is unrestricted. Validity then means almost nothing.

required_inputs.notes: Validate each call's arguments. A turn with no call is excluded unless the gold required a call, in which case it fails.

computation.formula: schema_valid = calls whose arguments validate / calls. Case score is 1 only if every call in the case validates.
procedure: Parse structured tool calls.
Validate arguments with the tool schema.
Use the case-level all-valid bit as the gate statistic.
implementations: BFCL AST checks include a looser structural cousin

interpretation.meaning: Every call's arguments matched the schema.
The default gate for unattended execution.
No call validated.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 for tools that execute unattended.

cost_effort.notes: Free, and it should be a gate whenever tools have schemas.

limitations: Schema-valid arguments can still be the wrong values. Pair with tool_call_correct or task success.
Providers sometimes repair arguments before you see them. Record whether you score the raw or repaired call.
provenance: BIY agent gate on tool arguments

metrics.name: Tool-call match
metrics.description: The predicted tool call matches the expected call on name and arguments, using the BFCL abstract-syntax match: arguments are equal under the documented normalizer, and parallel calls match as a set. This is the catalogue metric tool_call_correct. It is the default when the correct call is known.
metrics.measures: Whether the model emitted the expected tool call, including arguments.

signals: The request includes a tool or function schema
A fixture records the correct call
The product executes the call without a human rewrite

when_not_to_use: Several different calls are legitimately correct. Exact AST match will under-score. Prefer agent_task_success on the resulting state, or list the acceptable calls.
You only care which tool was chosen, not the arguments. tool_choice_correct is the smaller metric.

required_inputs.notes: Config allows argument aliases and numeric tolerance. Parallel calls are order-insensitive. Catalogue id tool_call_correct.

computation.formula: score = 1 if the predicted call set matches an acceptable gold call set under AST equality, else 0.
procedure: Parse the tool call from the provider's tool-call object, not from prose.
Match names and arguments against the acceptable gold sets.
Average over cases. A parse failure is a miss.

interpretation.meaning: Every case emitted an acceptable call.
Strong single-step calling. Inspect argument mismatches before gating lower.
No case matched.

score.aggregation: Mean of per-case matches. Report name-only accuracy beside it.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.95 when the call is executed unattended and the gold call is unique.

cost_effort.notes: Free given fixtures. The cost is writing acceptable calls.

limitations: AST match rejects equivalent arguments that the normalizer does not know, such as a reordered filter list.
Provider tool-call formats differ. A parser bug looks like a model failure. Keep the parser pinned.

metrics.name: Tool-call F1
metrics.description: Precision and recall over the set of tool calls when more than one call is required. Ragas tool-call F1 and a set F1 on (name, canonical arguments) are the same idea. Use it for parallel and multi-call turns where a single exact match hides partial success.
metrics.measures: Set overlap between predicted and gold calls.

signals: Gold labels contain more than one call
Exact match is zero for models that get most of the calls right
You want a quality term with partial credit

when_not_to_use: A partial call set is still a failed action, such as a payment that needed every step. Use the exact match or the end state.
There is a single call. tool_call_correct is clearer.

required_inputs.notes: Calls are matched on name plus canonical arguments. Config can match on name only.

computation.formula: P = |pred ∩ gold| / |pred|, R = |pred ∩ gold| / |gold|, F1 = 2PR/(P+R). Empty gold and empty pred score 1.
procedure: Canonicalize calls.
Compute set F1.
Average over turns.

interpretation.meaning: The call sets match.
Partial overlap. Read precision versus recall to see extra calls versus missed calls.
No overlap, or the model called tools when the gold set was empty.

cost_effort.notes: Free once the gold call labels exist. No extra model call.

limitations: Partial credit can rank a model that never completes a task above one that does, if you are not careful. Check task success.
Argument canonicalization decides the score. Publish the normalizer version.

metrics.name: Tool choice
metrics.description: Whether the model selected the right tool, or correctly selected none. Arguments are ignored. This is the catalogue metric tool_choice_correct. Use it when the routing decision is the product question and arguments are checked separately or not at all.
metrics.measures: Correctness of the tool name, including the decision to call nothing.

signals: Multiple tools are available
Calling the wrong API has a cost even with good arguments
Some requests should produce no call

when_not_to_use: Arguments are the actual risk, such as a payment amount. tool_call_correct or argument checks must lead.
Any of several tools can do the job. A single gold name is the wrong label. Score the end state.

required_inputs.notes: Gold may be a tool name or none. Config decides whether parallel calls must include all gold names.

computation.formula: score = 1 if the set of called tool names equals the gold set, else 0. The empty set is a legitimate gold.
procedure: Read tool names from the structured tool-call field.
Compare to the gold set.
Average. Break out misses on the no-call subset.
implementations: BFCL relevance and irrelevance splits, simplified

interpretation.meaning: Every case called the right names, including correct abstentions.
Routing is mostly right. Check the no-call slice before trusting the average.
No case selected the right set.

score.aggregation: Mean over cases, with the abstention slice reported.

cost_effort.notes: Negligible next to the model call. No judge and no extra request.

limitations: A right name with a dangerous argument scores 1. Do not use this as the only agent metric.
Synonymous tools in the catalog make the gold name arbitrary.

metrics.name: Tool-error recovery
metrics.description: After a tool returns an error the agent can do something about, the share of episodes that still reach the goal or surface the error correctly instead of looping, ignoring it, or inventing a result. Use it when production tools are flaky or the agent must handle bad arguments.
metrics.measures: Behavior after a recoverable tool error.

signals: Tool traces contain errors and retries
The agent sometimes fabricates a result after a 4xx or 5xx
You can inject a recoverable fault in the sandbox

when_not_to_use: Tools in the benchmark never fail. The metric is undefined. Do not score the happy path as recovery.
The error is not recoverable. The correct behavior is to stop and tell the user, which is a policy check, not a retry score.

required_inputs.notes: The harness injects a labeled recoverable fault. Gold behavior is either eventual success or a correct explanation, as labeled per item.

computation.formula: recovery = episodes with the labeled correct post-error behavior / episodes with an injected fault.
procedure: Inject the fault at a defined step.
Run until stop or a step cap.
Score success against the labeled recovery behavior. Count infinite retries as failure.
implementations: BFCL missing-parameter and error-recovery style splits

interpretation.meaning: Every injected fault was handled as labeled.
Half the faults are mishandled. Do not let this agent call side-effecting tools alone.
No fault was handled correctly.

cost_effort.notes: Run on a small fault set, not on every case.

limitations: The fault taxonomy is the evaluation. A model tuned to your injector may still fail on real faults.
Retry storms can look like persistence. Cap steps.
provenance: BFCL multi-turn error and missing-argument splits

metrics.name: Ambiguous-context bias
metrics.description: On questions where the context does not determine the answer, how strongly the model picks a stereotype-consistent answer instead of 'unknown'. BBQ's bias score for ambiguous contexts is this metric. The ideal is zero. A model can be accurate on clear questions and still fail here.
metrics.measures: Stereotype-aligned choices when the evidence does not support a choice.

use_cases: QA and classification in hiring, credit, care, or moderation
any prompt that includes people and an underspecified question
signals: Outputs are decisions about people
Contexts are sometimes incomplete
The client is worried about stereotyping

when_not_to_use: The task never involves demographic groups. A BBQ-style set would be an artificial add-on. Skip it.
You only report overall accuracy. Accuracy can hide bias on the ambiguous slice. If you run this, keep the slice separate.

required_inputs.notes: Items follow the BBQ pattern: a context, a question, and an unknown option. The evaluation set is a reviewed benchmark, not a production log of real people.

computation.formula: s = 2 * (n_stereotype_aligned / n_non_unknown) - 1 on ambiguous items. bias_score = (1 - accuracy) * s. The stored score is bias_score, in [-1, 1], and 0 is best.
procedure: Score ambiguous items only.
Compute accuracy, treating 'unknown' as correct.
Compute the scaled bias score. Also publish disambiguated accuracy so a model cannot win by answering unknown to everything.

interpretation.meaning: No measured stereotype preference on ambiguous items.
A detectable lean. Read the category breakdown before treating it as noise.
When the model does not abstain, it always picks the stereotype-aligned answer, and it is wrong.

score.aggregation: Mean bias score by demographic category. Do not bury a category in a global average.

cost_effort.notes: The set is the cost. Scoring is exact match against the unknown label plus the bias formula.

limitations: BBQ categories do not cover every group or every country. A clean score is not a clean product.
The score is a property of the item set. Do not compare across different ambiguous sets.

metrics.name: Counterfactual invariance
metrics.description: The share of items whose decision stays the same when a demographic mention that should be irrelevant is swapped: names, pronouns, or group terms. HELM's counterfactual fairness check is this idea. Higher is better. Use it on client decisions such as triage, hiring screens, and credit language.
metrics.measures: Stability of a decision under irrelevant demographic swaps.

signals: The decision should not depend on a protected attribute
You can rewrite the attribute and keep the rest of the case
Stakeholders ask for a fairness check that is about their workflow

when_not_to_use: The attribute is legitimately relevant to the correct answer, as in a clinical fact. Invariance would punish accuracy.
You cannot generate a careful counterfactual. A sloppy rewrite changes more than the attribute and the score is junk.

required_inputs.notes: Pairs are prewritten. The scorer does not invent new demographic tests at runtime. Compare normalized decisions, not full prose, unless the product ships the prose unchanged.

computation.formula: invariance = pairs whose normalized decisions match / pairs.
procedure: Run each pair.
Normalize the decision to the label or the extracted field.
Score equality. Report the direction of disagreements.

interpretation.meaning: No decision changed under the swaps.
Most decisions are stable. Review the disagreements. They are the finding.
Decisions flip on half the pairs. Do not ship as an unattended decision aid.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.98 for unattended decisions that policy says must be invariant.

cost_effort.notes: Use a small, reviewed pair set. Quality of the rewrite dominates the statistic.

limitations: Invariance does not mean the decision is good. A model can be consistently wrong.
Name swaps carry cultural stereotypes of their own. Document the name list.

metrics.name: Equalized-odds gap
metrics.description: The maximum gap in true positive rate or false positive rate across groups for a classifier. Lower is better. Use it when the model assigns a label that triggers an action and group labels exist on a properly collected evaluation set. Do not compute it by inferring sensitive attributes from names in production logs.
metrics.measures: The gap in true-positive and false-positive rates across groups.

signals: The model is a classifier with material outcomes
Group labels exist on a consented evaluation set
False positives and false negatives both have a defined cost

when_not_to_use: You would infer race, gender, or health status from text to create the groups. Do not.
Base rates differ and the client has chosen a different fairness criterion, such as calibration within groups. Equalized odds may be the wrong target. Say which criterion you were asked for.

required_inputs.notes: subgroup_labels must come from an authorized evaluation set, not from a guesser model.

computation.formula: gap = max over group pairs of max(|TPR_a - TPR_b|, |FPR_a - FPR_b|). Range 0–1. Lower is better.
procedure: Compute TPR and FPR per group.
Take the maximum absolute gap.
Publish the per-group rates. The gap alone is not actionable.

interpretation.meaning: TPR and FPR match across the groups you measured.
A 10 point error gap. Material for an eligibility decision. Confirm sample size.
Some group has an error rate at the opposite extreme of another.

score.aggregation: One gap per positive class, with confidence intervals.

cost_effort.driver: Confusion matrices on a labeled set.
cost_effort.notes: The statistic is cheap. The authorized data is the constraint.

limitations: Small groups make the gap noisy. Report intervals.
Satisfying equalized odds can conflict with calibration and with accuracy. The client has to pick.

metrics.name: Representation skew
metrics.description: How far the distribution of groups in the model's generations sits from a reference distribution the client chose, using total variation distance. Lower is better. HELM reports demographic representation in generations. The reference is a product decision, such as the customer base, and must be written down.
metrics.measures: Distance between generated group frequencies and a reference distribution.

use_cases: examples and stock text that should not collapse to one demographic
signals: The model invents people
A reference distribution exists
Stakeholders care who shows up in examples

when_not_to_use: There is no agreed reference distribution. Distance to a distribution you invented is not a fairness result.
The task is extraction from a source. The source's distribution is the right one. Skew versus the population would punish faithfulness.

required_inputs.notes: labels holds the reference distribution. Generations are labeled by a pinned classifier or by the names the model used. Document which.

computation.formula: TVD = 0.5 * sum_g |p_model(g) - p_reference(g)|. Range 0–1. Lower is better.
procedure: Label a large enough sample of invented entities.
Estimate the model distribution.
Compute total variation against the frozen reference. Report counts, not only the distance.

interpretation.meaning: The generated distribution matches the reference.
A substantial shift. Look at which groups are missing.
The distributions are disjoint.

score.aggregation: One distance per attribute, with bootstrap intervals because counts are small.

cost_effort.notes: Needs enough samples to estimate a distribution. Do not compute it on twenty rows.

limitations: The reference is normative. State who chose it.
Name-based gender and ethnicity inference is error-prone. Prefer explicit self-descriptions in a controlled prompt.

metrics.name: Stereotype rate
metrics.description: The share of generations that a pinned stereotype or regard classifier flags, or that contain a listed stereotype pattern, when the prompt mentions a group. Lower is better. HELM's bias metrics on generated text are the ancestor. This is about what the model says, not about decision invariance.
metrics.measures: Stereotype-bearing content in generations about groups.

signals: The model generates descriptions of people or groups
You have a classifier or a reviewed pattern list
Decision invariance does not cover free text

when_not_to_use: The task is a classification decision. Use counterfactual_invariance or equalized_odds_gap.
The classifier is known to fire on neutral identity mentions. Calibrate it or you will punish naming a group at all.

required_inputs.notes: The classifier slot may be a regard or stereotype model rather than Perspective. Pin it. Prompts are a reviewed set, not live user data about real individuals.

computation.formula: stereotype_rate = flagged_generations / generations. Lower is better.
procedure: Run the reviewed prompt set.
Score each generation.
Report the rate by group. A gap between groups is the finding, not only the mean.
implementations: BOLD and StereoSet-style prompts with a documented scorer

interpretation.meaning: Nothing was flagged. Confirm the classifier actually fires on a positive control.
A tenth of generations were flagged. Inspect before calling it bias or classifier noise.
Every generation was flagged.

score.aggregation: Mean, plus the max-minus-min gap across groups.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap once the prompt set exists. Budget a human audit of flags.

limitations: Stereotype classifiers disagree and encode their own biases.
A low rate can mean the model refused to discuss groups, which may or may not be acceptable.

metrics.name: Subgroup performance gap
metrics.description: The difference between the best and worst subgroup on the task's primary quality metric. Lower is better. Subgroups may be languages, dialects, regions, or authorized demographic slices. HELM's performance-disparity fairness check is this pattern. It shows a model that looks fine on average and fails a group the client serves.
metrics.measures: The spread of task quality across subgroups.

signals: The product serves more than one language or segment
Average quality can hide a weak segment
You can label the segment without guessing a sensitive attribute

when_not_to_use: Segments would be inferred sensitive attributes. Refuse the metric rather than infer them.
A subgroup has too few items to estimate quality. Report that instead of a gap.

required_inputs.notes: The primary metric is whichever quality metric was selected for the task. This metric is the gap of that metric. Minimum support per subgroup is configurable and defaults to 30.

computation.formula: gap = max_g Q_g - min_g Q_g, on subgroups meeting the support floor. Lower is better. Range depends on Q. We store it on the same 0–1 scale as Q.
procedure: Compute the primary quality metric within each subgroup.
Drop subgroups below the support floor and list them.
Report the max-min gap and the identity of the worst subgroup.

interpretation.meaning: Every measured subgroup has the same quality.
A 10 point quality gap. Often enough to change which model you ship for the worst slice.
Some subgroup is at the floor and another at the ceiling of Q.

score.aggregation: One gap per run, worst subgroup named.
score.suggested_gate: The worst subgroup still clears the product's quality floor. The gap itself is not the gate.

cost_effort.driver: Slicing a metric you already computed.
cost_effort.notes: Free given labels. Collecting the slice labels is the work.

limitations: Max-min ignores subgroup size. A tiny slice can dominate. The support floor is there for that reason.
Closing the gap by degrading the best group is not a product win. Watch the level, not only the gap.

metrics.name: Containment rate
metrics.description: The share of conversations resolved without a human handoff. It is the standard support-deflection number. Higher is not automatically better: a bot that traps people inflates containment and destroys satisfaction. Read it next to escalation quality and a repeat-contact check.
metrics.measures: Conversations that end without a handoff to a human agent.

signals: There is a handoff to a human agent
The business case is deflection

when_not_to_use: There is no human queue. Containment is undefined.
As the only success metric. Pair it with conversation_completeness or repeat contact, or you will reward trapping the user.

required_inputs.notes: A contained conversation has no handoff. Config window defines a recontact that retroactively breaks containment.

computation.formula: containment = conversations with no handoff and no recontact in the window / conversations.
procedure: Join chats to handoff events.
Apply the recontact window.
Report raw no-handoff rate and the recontact-adjusted rate. The adjusted rate is the one to show.
implementations: Deflection rate with a recontact window

interpretation.meaning: A high deflection rate that is only good if recontact and CSAT hold.
Most chats still reach a person. The bot may still be saving time. Check handle time.

cost_effort.notes: Free if the contact platform logs handoffs. The interpretation is the hard part.

limitations: Policy that makes handoff difficult inflates the rate.
Containment can rise while correctness falls. Keep a quality metric.

metrics.name: CSAT
metrics.description: The mean customer satisfaction score on chats the model handled, on the client's existing survey scale, normalized to 0–1. It is a business outcome. It moves for reasons that have nothing to do with the model, including queue time and who was surveyed. Use it as a guarded outcome, not as Q.
metrics.measures: Survey satisfaction on model-handled contacts.

use_cases: comparing a bot with the prior human or bot baseline
signals: A CSAT survey already runs
The business case cites satisfaction

when_not_to_use: There is no survey. Do not synthesize CSAT from a judge.
As a model-quality term in Q. Too many confounders.

required_inputs.notes: Normalize the client's scale to 0–1 for storage and show the original scale in the report. Publish the response rate.

computation.formula: csat_norm = (mean_score - scale_min) / (scale_max - scale_min).
procedure: Restrict the sample to contacts the model actually handled, with the handling rule written down.
Compute the mean on the original scale and the normalized value.
Compare to the baseline period. Do not rank offline candidates by a survey they were not in.

interpretation.meaning: A strong score on a typical normalized scale. Confirm the original instrument.
The deployment is losing satisfaction. This is a business stop signal, not a fine-grained model rank.

score.aggregation: Mean over responses, with the response rate.

cost_effort.notes: Free as a deployment monitor. Not available at offline candidate-selection time unless you run a live test.

limitations: Confounded by wait time, policy, and survey bias.
Offline benchmarks do not produce CSAT. Do not pretend a rubric is CSAT.

metrics.name: Escalation rate
metrics.description: The share of conversations handed to a human. Lower is not always better. For safety and eligibility, a missed escalation is the failure. Report the rate and, where labels exist, whether the escalation was appropriate. This is the complement of raw containment before the recontact adjustment.
metrics.measures: How often the assistant hands the conversation to a human.

use_cases: clinical and financial flows that must escalate
signals: Handoff exists
Some situations must escalate
Containment is on the dashboard

when_not_to_use: You wanted appropriateness, but you only have the rate. Do not call a low rate 'good escalation'.
As a second term in a score beside containment. They move together. Pick one and explain the recontact rule.

required_inputs.notes: Handoff events. Optional labels of whether the handoff was required.

computation.formula: escalation_rate = conversations with a handoff / conversations. If required-escalation labels exist, also report recall of those cases.
procedure: Count handoffs.
If you have labels for must-escalate cases, compute recall separately.
Do not set a lower-is-better gate unless product and risk both agree.

interpretation.meaning: The bot is failing to hand off. That is a risk miss, not a containment win.
The bot is not containing the traffic it was bought for.

score.aggregation: Pooled rate, plus recall on the must-escalate slice when labeled.
score.suggested_gate: Recall of must-escalate cases >= a client threshold. The overall rate is not a gate.

cost_effort.notes: Free given handoff events.

limitations: The overall rate has no universal direction.
Users demanding a human are not the same as cases the policy says must escalate.

metrics.name: Human acceptance rate
metrics.description: The share of outputs a person accepts without a material edit, or with an edit below a configured distance. This is the ground truth for drafting tools: suggestions, replies, and summaries a human must approve. It is expensive and it is the metric that calibrates the judge.
metrics.measures: Whether a person kept the model's output.

signals: A person reviews the output before it ships
Accept or edit events are logged
You want to calibrate rubric_score against people

when_not_to_use: Nothing is logged and you cannot afford a review panel. A judge is not this metric. Do not rename a rubric to acceptance.
Reviewers are graded on speed and accept everything. The rate then measures the reviewer, not the model.

required_inputs.notes: An acceptance event from production is better than a lab panel, if the UI actually lets people edit. Config max_edit_distance defines material edit.

computation.formula: acceptance = outputs accepted with normalized edit distance <= max_distance / reviewed outputs.
procedure: Define a material edit.
Count acceptances in production or in a blind review.
Report reviewer agreement if you use a panel.

interpretation.meaning: Four in five drafts are kept. Strong for a suggestion UI, and a number you should check against thumbs and edits.
Most drafts are rewritten. The model is a rough starter, not a replacement.

cost_effort.driver: Human review or a production sample large enough to estimate the rate.
cost_effort.notes: The expensive metric. Use it to calibrate the judge on a sample, then judge the rest.

limitations: Reviewer taste and incentives dominate.
A UI that makes editing hard inflates acceptance.

metrics.name: Normalized edit distance
metrics.description: The normalized Levenshtein distance between the model draft and the text a person finally sent. Lower is better. It is the continuous companion of acceptance. A draft that is accepted after a one-word fix should not look like a draft that was rewritten.
metrics.measures: How much a person changed the draft before sending.

signals: The final sent text is logged next to the draft
Acceptance alone hides heavy edits

when_not_to_use: People send the draft unchanged or not at all, and you do not have the edited text. You only have acceptance.
As the only quality metric for factual tasks. A fluent wrong answer can be sent unchanged.

required_inputs.notes: The final text is the production outcome. Distance is characters or tokens, pinned, divided by the length of the longer string.

computation.formula: distance = levenshtein(draft, final) / max(len(draft), len(final), 1). Range 0–1. Lower is better. Empty final after a draft counts as 1.
procedure: Join draft to the sent text.
Compute normalized distance.
Report the median. The mean is dominated by full rewrites.

interpretation.meaning: The sent text matched the draft.
A light edit. Often still a useful draft.
A full rewrite or a discarded draft.

score.aggregation: Median over drafts that were edited or sent.

cost_effort.driver: String distance on logs you have.
cost_effort.notes: Free given the join. The logging is the cost.

limitations: Character distance treats a factual correction like a stylistic one.
Reviewers who delete and retype the same sentence inflate the distance.

metrics.name: Readability band match
metrics.description: The share of outputs whose reading grade falls inside a band the client set, such as a patient-education or consumer-finance reading level. It uses a deterministic readability formula. It is not a measure of truth or of tone.
metrics.measures: Whether the text lands in the requested reading-level band.

signals: The brief names a grade level or plain language
The audience is not specialists
Reviewers reject text as too dense

when_not_to_use: The audience is expert and density is appropriate. A low grade level would be a worse answer.
The language is not supported by the formula you have. Flesch is an English formula. Do not report it for other languages.

required_inputs.notes: Config is the minimum and maximum US grade level. Default formula is Flesch-Kincaid grade for English. Pin the formula.

computation.formula: score = 1 if min_grade <= flesch_kincaid_grade(text) <= max_grade else 0. Grade = 0.39 * (words/sentences) + 11.8 * (syllables/words) - 15.59.
procedure: Compute the grade with a pinned implementation.
Test the band.
Average. Also report the median grade so a miss is interpretable.

interpretation.meaning: Every output fell in the band.
Half the outputs are outside the requested level.

score.aggregation: Mean of in-band bits, plus median grade.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.9 when a reading level is a stated requirement of the communication.

cost_effort.notes: Very cheap. Do not pay a judge to guess the grade.

limitations: Grade level is a rough proxy. Short sentences full of jargon can score as easy.
The formula is English-specific.

metrics.name: Regeneration rate
metrics.description: The share of turns where the user asked for another answer. Lower usually means the first answer was enough. It is a behavioral signal, cheaper than a rating and still biased by users who never regenerate because they simply leave.
metrics.measures: How often a user explicitly asks the product to generate again.

signals: The UI has a regenerate or retry control
Events are logged

when_not_to_use: The product regenerates automatically. Those retries are not user dissatisfaction.
As a quality score for short labels. Nobody regenerates a classification. The event does not exist.

required_inputs.notes: Count explicit user regenerations, not client retries on HTTP errors.

computation.formula: regeneration_rate = turns with a user regeneration / turns.
procedure: Count regenerate events.
Exclude automatic retries.
Report the rate next to acceptance if both exist.

interpretation.meaning: One in twenty turns is regenerated. A useful trend line, not a verdict.
Users often reject the first answer. Read the transcripts.

cost_effort.notes: Free if the event exists.

limitations: Power users regenerate more. Segment if you can.
A missing regenerate button does not mean people were happy.

metrics.name: Thumbs-up rate
metrics.description: The share of rated outputs that received a positive rating. It is a production signal, biased by who bothers to rate. Use it as a trend and a calibration check, not as the metric you optimize a model against directly.
metrics.measures: Positive ratings among outputs that received a rating.

use_cases: chat products with a thumb widget
spotting a regression the offline set missed
signals: The product already collects thumbs
You want a production comparator

when_not_to_use: As the sole launch metric. Response rates are low and angry users are over-represented.
To train the model online without a review. Thumbs are easy to game and easy to misread.

required_inputs.notes: Denominator is rated outputs, not all outputs. Always publish the rating rate beside the thumbs-up rate.

computation.formula: thumbs_up_rate = positive_ratings / ratings.
procedure: Count ratings in a pre-registered window.
Compute the positive share and the rating rate.
Do not compare two models with very different rating rates as if the thumbs were unbiased.

interpretation.meaning: High among people who rated. Check how few that is.
Split ratings. Read the written comments if you have them.

cost_effort.notes: Free if the widget exists. Not a reason to add a widget only for the benchmark.

limitations: Selection bias is severe.
A model that refuses more often can get fewer angry thumbs and look better.
provenance: LMSYS-style human preference is the cleaner paired version

metrics.name: Brand-voice fit
