metrics.description: A rubric, grounded in the client's brand guidelines, scores whether the output sounds like the brand. This is the catalogue metric tone_brand_fit. It is a quality term only when a written guide exists. Without a guide the judge invents a voice and the score is not comparable.
metrics.measures: Match to a written brand voice, not generic pleasantness.

signals: A brand guide or voice spec is in the repo or attached to the use case
The output is customer-visible
Reviewers reject drafts for voice rather than facts

when_not_to_use: There is no written guide. Do not ask a judge whether the text 'sounds on brand'.
The failure is a banned phrase. contains_none is deterministic. Use the rubric for voice that a word list cannot capture.

required_inputs.notes: The brand guide is required. The rubric is drafted from it, with anchored examples. Catalogue id tone_brand_fit.

computation.formula: Normalized rubric score on 0–1. Use the g_eval probability-weighted form when logprobs exist.
procedure: Draft a short rubric from the guide: voice, formality, and things the brand never says.
Score each output. Ignore factual errors here.
Calibrate against a small human sample before weighting it heavily in Q.
implementations: A G-Eval rubric over the brand guide

interpretation.meaning: The top anchor of the brand rubric.
Recognizably the brand with some misses. Read the misses before treating the gap as model quality.
The bottom anchor.

cost_effort.notes: Worth it for customer-visible copy. Skip for internal JSON.

limitations: Judges regress to a generic professional voice. The anchors have to be specific.
Brand fit can be high on a factually wrong or unsafe answer. It does not replace those metrics.

metrics.name: Brier score
metrics.description: The mean squared error between a predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome. Lower is better. It penalizes both miscalibration and poor discrimination, and it is a proper scoring rule, unlike accuracy. Use it for binary risk flags when the model exposes a probability.
metrics.measures: Squared error of predicted probabilities.

signals: The model outputs a probability for a binary event
You will rank on the probability, not only on a hard label
A proper scoring rule was requested

when_not_to_use: The model outputs only a label. Brier needs a probability. Accuracy or F1 is the label metric.
The outcome is multiclass and you have not defined a one-versus-rest reduction. Do that explicitly or use ECE.

required_inputs.notes: confidence is the predicted probability of the positive class. labels are 0 or 1.

computation.formula: Brier = mean((p_i - y_i)^2). Range 0–1. Lower is better.
procedure: Collect probabilities and outcomes.
Average the squared errors.
Compare with the Brier score of the base-rate predictor so a low number is not just a rare event.

interpretation.meaning: Every probability was exactly the outcome.
No better than predicting 0.5 on a balanced problem. Always compare with the base-rate Brier score.
Every probability was exactly wrong.

cost_effort.notes: Free given probabilities.

limitations: A lower Brier score does not say whether the remaining error is calibration or resolution. ECE splits calibration out.
Probabilities from a verbalized percentage are not comparable to logprobs.

metrics.name: Expected calibration error
metrics.description: The average gap between the model's confidence and its accuracy, weighted by how many predictions fall in each confidence bin. HELM reports calibration beside accuracy. Lower is better. Use token probabilities when they exist, and verbalized confidence only with that choice recorded. A confident wrong extractor is worse than an uncertain one.
metrics.measures: Mismatch between stated confidence and observed accuracy.

use_cases: any decision that will be automated above a threshold
signals: The product uses a confidence threshold
Logprobs or a verbalized probability are available
Wrong and confident is worse than wrong and unsure

when_not_to_use: You have no confidence signal. Do not invent one by asking the model 'how sure are you' and then treat it as a probability without a calibration set.
The task is open-ended generation with no correctness bit. ECE needs a correct or incorrect label.

required_inputs.notes: Prefer the probability of the chosen label from logprobs. Verbalized confidence is a different measurement and must be named in the run.

computation.formula: ECE = sum_b (n_b / n) * |acc(b) - conf(b)| over equal-width bins. Default is 10 bins. Lower is better.
procedure: Pair each prediction's confidence with its correctness bit.
Bin confidences.
Compute the weighted absolute gap. Plot a reliability diagram. The number without the diagram is easy to overread.

interpretation.meaning: Accuracy matches confidence in every occupied bin.
A 10 point average gap. Thresholds set from raw confidence will be wrong.
Confidence and accuracy are maximally apart on the binning used.

score.aggregation: One ECE per candidate. Also report the count per bin.

cost_effort.driver: Binning arithmetic on labels you already scored.
cost_effort.notes: Free given confidences and correctness. Collecting logprobs has a small provider cost.

limitations: ECE depends on the number of bins and the sample size. Publish both.
Verbalized confidence is not a probability. Do not compare it with logprob ECE.

metrics.name: Hallucination rate
metrics.description: The share of outputs that contain at least one factual claim unsupported by the designated source. This is the catalogue metric hallucination. It is the case-level, lower-better companion of faithfulness. A single invented sentence fails the output even if the rest is supported. Use it as a gate. Put faithfulness, not this rate, into the quality average.
metrics.measures: Whether an output contains any unsupported factual claim.

use_cases: answers that must stick to a chart, policy, or ticket
signals: A source is logged with the output
One invented fact fails the product even if the rest is right
You already understand faithfulness and want a harder case-level gate

when_not_to_use: There is no source. Calling world-knowledge errors 'hallucination' without a key mixes this up with factual_correctness. Use that, with a reference.
As a second quality term beside faithfulness. They are the same judgments aggregated differently. Gate on this, average faithfulness.

required_inputs.notes: Same claim split as faithfulness. An output with no factual claims is not a hallucination. Catalogue id hallucination.

computation.formula: hallucination = outputs with at least one unsupported claim / outputs. Lower is better.
procedure: Split claims the same way as faithfulness.
Fail the output if any claim is unsupported.
Report the rate and do not also enter it into Q.
implementations: HaluEval-style labels where a human key exists

interpretation.meaning: No output contained an unsupported claim.
One in twenty outputs invents something. Often too high for a clinical or legal answer.
Every output contained an unsupported claim.

score.suggested_gate: <= 0.02 for customer-visible regulated answers, using the client's source.

cost_effort.driver: The same judge pass as faithfulness.
cost_effort.notes: Free if faithfulness verdicts are stored. Do not pay a second judge.

limitations: Any-claim failure is harsh on long answers. That is intentional for a gate and wrong as the only quality number.
The metric inherits the judge's blind spots on numbers.
provenance: Ragas faithfulness aggregated at case level

metrics.name: Overconfidence rate
metrics.description: The share of incorrect answers whose confidence is at or above a high threshold. Lower is better. ECE summarizes the whole reliability curve. This metric isolates the failure mode that hurts automation: wrong and sure.
metrics.measures: How often the model is confidently wrong.

use_cases: customer-visible answers with a confidence badge
signals: A confidence value is shown or used
High-confidence errors are the incident type
You have correctness labels

when_not_to_use: There is no confidence. Do not ask for a one-off verbalized score only to feed this metric unless you will calibrate it.
You wanted the full reliability picture. Use expected_calibration_error.

required_inputs.notes: Config threshold defaults to 0.8. Correctness comes from the task metric's pass bit.

computation.formula: overconfidence = incorrect items with confidence >= threshold / all items. Lower is better. Also report the rate among incorrect items.
procedure: Join confidence to the correctness bit.
Count high-confidence errors.
Publish both denominators so a rare error class is visible.
implementations: A high-confidence error rate beside ECE

interpretation.meaning: No incorrect answer was emitted above the threshold.
Two percent of items are confident and wrong. Often too many for unattended posting.
Every item was a high-confidence error.

score.suggested_gate: <= 0.01 when high-confidence outputs post automatically.

cost_effort.driver: A join of scores you have.
cost_effort.notes: Free given confidence and correctness.

limitations: The threshold is arbitrary. Sweep it before freezing a gate.
A model can hide overconfidence by never being confident, and then selective coverage collapses.

metrics.name: Selective accuracy
metrics.description: Accuracy on the items the model chose to answer, reported with the coverage of that choice. A model can look accurate by abstaining on the hard items. The pair (coverage, selective accuracy) is the metric. Use it when the product is allowed to defer to a human.
metrics.measures: Accuracy among answered items, together with how often the model answers.

signals: The product can abstain or escalate
Automation is allowed only above a confidence threshold
Headline accuracy is being gamed by refusals

when_not_to_use: The product must answer every item. Coverage is fixed at 1 and selective accuracy is just accuracy.
There is no correctness label on the answered slice.

required_inputs.notes: Config is the deferral rule: a confidence threshold or an explicit abstention label. Store coverage next to accuracy.

computation.formula: coverage = answered / all. selective_accuracy = correct_answered / answered. The stored score is selective accuracy, and coverage is a required companion statistic.
procedure: Apply the deferral rule.
Compute coverage and accuracy on the remainder.
Plot accuracy against coverage by sweeping the threshold. A single point hides the trade-off.

interpretation.meaning: Every answered item was correct. Coverage may still be tiny. Read coverage.
A plausible automation target. The numbers only make sense as a pair.
Nothing the model agreed to answer was correct.

score.aggregation: One accuracy and one coverage per threshold.
score.suggested_gate: selective accuracy >= the automation bar at the coverage the operations team requires.

cost_effort.notes: Free given a deferral rule and correctness.

limitations: Reporting accuracy without coverage is misleading. The schema's companion statistic is mandatory in the report.
The threshold is a product parameter. Do not tune it on the test set and then quote the test number.

metrics.name: Semantic entropy
metrics.description: Entropy of the distribution over meanings, estimated by clustering sampled answers that say the same thing. High entropy means the model is unstable about the meaning, which Farquhar and colleagues showed is a hallucination signal that does not need a gold answer. It is a diagnostic, not a quality score.
metrics.measures: Uncertainty over semantic clusters of sampled answers.

use_cases: deciding when to abstain without a gold label
signals: You can afford several samples
Gold labels are scarce
You want a hallucination signal that is not a judge of the source

when_not_to_use: As the quality metric. High confidence in a wrong answer has low entropy. Pair with a correctness or grounding metric.
The task is open-ended and many meanings are acceptable. Entropy will be high for good reasons.

required_inputs.notes: Cluster samples by bidirectional entailment or by a pinned equivalence judge. Embeddings alone are a weaker clusterer and must be labeled if used.

computation.formula: H = - sum_c p_c log p_c, where p_c is the fraction of samples in semantic cluster c. The stored value is H / log(n) so it lies in 0–1. Higher means more semantic disagreement.
procedure: Draw n samples.
Cluster by meaning.
Compute normalized entropy. Use it to rank uncertainty, not correctness.
implementations: SelfCheckGPT is the related consistency check

interpretation.meaning: All samples said the same thing. They can still be wrong.
Meaning is spread across clusters. A bad candidate for unattended factual use.
Every sample landed in its own meaning cluster.

cost_effort.notes: Expensive. Use on a sample of items, not the full set, unless the decision needs it.

limitations: Low entropy is not truth.
The clusterer is part of the metric. A loose clusterer understates uncertainty.

metrics.name: Unit-test pass rate
metrics.description: The share of hidden or visible unit tests the candidate code passes. This is the pass@1 form of functional correctness and the catalogue metric code_tests_pass. It is the default code-quality score when tests exist.
metrics.measures: Functional correctness against tests, not style and not security.

signals: The repo has tests that define success
The model is asked to write or edit code
A sandbox can run those tests

when_not_to_use: There are no tests and writing them is out of scope. A rubric on code is a weak substitute. Say so, and prefer syntax_valid_rate only as a floor.
The tests are shown to the model and it can hard-code them. Hidden tests, or tests written after the prompt is frozen, are required.

required_inputs.notes: Run in a sandbox with network disabled unless the test needs it. Pin the language runtime. Catalogue id code_tests_pass.

computation.formula: pass_rate = passed_tests / tests. A case-level alternate is 1 only if all tests pass. Use the case-level bit when any failure means the patch is useless, and the rate when partial credit matches the product.
procedure: Extract code from the model output.
Run the configured tests in the sandbox with a timeout.
Record pass, fail, timeout, and harness error separately. Harness errors are not model failures.

interpretation.meaning: Every test passed.
Most behavior is right. Read the failing assertions before shipping.
No test passed, or the code did not run.

score.aggregation: Mean of per-case all-tests-pass bits by default. Config can switch to micro over tests.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 when the generated code is applied automatically.

cost_effort.driver: Sandbox execution, not an extra model call.
cost_effort.notes: Cheap compared with a judge, and much more valid. Budget timeouts so a hanging test does not stall the run.

limitations: Tests can be wrong or incomplete. A pass is not a proof of correctness.
Flaky tests make model comparisons noise. Quarantine flakes before ranking.

metrics.name: CodeBLEU
metrics.description: A weighted blend of n-gram match, weighted n-gram match, AST match, and data-flow match against a reference program. It is useful when no tests exist and a reference implementation does. It is weaker than executing tests and should not outrank code_tests_pass.
metrics.measures: Structural similarity to a reference program.

use_cases: code tasks that have a reference implementation and no executable tests
translation between languages with a reference
signals: A reference solution exists
Tests are unavailable
You want partial credit for almost-right structure

when_not_to_use: Tests run. Prefer code_tests_pass. Many correct programs look nothing like the reference.
It would be the sole launch metric. Structural similarity can be high for a subtly wrong program.

required_inputs.notes: Needs a parser for the language. Pin CodeBLEU weights and the parser version.

computation.formula: CodeBLEU = α·BLEU + β·BLEU_weighted + γ·AST_match + δ·dataflow_match, with the usual weights 0.25 each unless config overrides them.
procedure: Parse the candidate and the reference.
Compute the four components.
Combine with frozen weights. Publish components, not only the blend.

interpretation.meaning: The candidate matches the reference on n-grams, tree, and data flow.
Partial structural overlap. Not evidence the code works.
No measured overlap.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap next to execution, and less valid. Use it only as a stand-in.

limitations: A different correct algorithm scores poorly.
Language support is uneven. A failed parse must be a missing score, not a zero you hide.

metrics.name: Insecure-code rate
metrics.description: The share of generated programs that a pinned static-analysis policy flags for a security issue: injection, hard-coded secrets, unsafe deserialization, and the other rules in the configured ruleset. Lower is better. A passing test suite does not imply the code is safe to merge.
metrics.measures: Static-analysis findings in generated code under a frozen ruleset.

use_cases: code assistants that open pull requests
samples that junior developers might paste
signals: Generated code may be merged or run
The client has a SAST policy
You have seen secrets or injection in samples

when_not_to_use: The output is not code.
You treat a clean scan as proof of security. Static analysis misses logic flaws. It is a floor.

required_inputs.notes: Pin the analyzer and the ruleset hash. Config severity sets which findings count. Default is high and critical.

computation.formula: insecure_code_rate = outputs with at least one finding at or above the severity / outputs. Lower is better.
procedure: Extract code and write it to the sandbox.
Run the pinned analyzer.
Score the case as insecure if any finding meets the severity. Store rule ids.
implementations: Semgrep or Bandit with a pinned ruleset

interpretation.meaning: No output tripped the ruleset.
One in twenty samples has a finding. Too high for unattended merge.
Every output tripped the ruleset.

score.aggregation: Mean over outputs. Also report findings per thousand lines so length is visible.
score.suggested_gate: <= 0.01 before unattended merge, using the client's real ruleset.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap next to the test suite. Run it in the same sandbox job.

limitations: Rulesets have false positives. Triage the gate so a noisy rule does not eliminate every model.
A model can pass the ruleset and still implement the wrong, dangerous behavior.

metrics.name: pass@k
metrics.description: The probability that at least one of k independent samples passes the tests. The unbiased estimator draws n ≥ k samples and uses the Codex formula, which has lower variance than generating exactly k samples. Use it when a person or a harness will try several drafts. For a single shipped sample, use code_tests_pass.
metrics.measures: Coverage of tasks if the product can spend k samples and keep a passing one.

use_cases: code assistants that show several candidates
estimating the value of extra samples
signals: The product samples more than once or the user can regenerate
Tests can automatically pick a passing sample
You are deciding a sample budget

when_not_to_use: Production keeps one sample and a person does not sort through failures. pass@k flatters models that occasionally succeed. Report code_tests_pass or pass_hat_k.
You cannot execute tests. There is nothing to pass.

required_inputs.notes: n must be at least k. The same n samples can produce pass@1, pass@10, and pass_hat_k.

computation.formula: pass@k = mean over tasks of (1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k)), where c is the number of passing samples and C is the binomial coefficient. If n - c < k the term is 1.
procedure: Draw n samples per task and execute the tests on each.
Count passes c.
Apply the unbiased estimator. Do not use 1 - (1 - c/n)^k, which is biased low.

interpretation.meaning: Every task has at least one passing sample in a way that makes every k-subset succeed, or simply all samples pass.
Half the tasks are solvable within the sample budget, in expectation.
No task produced a passing sample.

score.aggregation: Unweighted mean of the unbiased per-task estimator.

cost_effort.driver: n samples per task, each executed.
cost_effort.notes: Do not use n=200 on a client set unless the decision depends on sample scaling. n equal to the product's real retry count is enough.

limitations: pass@k rises with k even when a single sample is unreliable. Read pass_hat_k for reliability.
The estimator assumes i.i.d. samples. Provider caching and fixed seeds break that.
provenance: Chen et al., 2021, evaluating large language models trained on code

metrics.name: Patch resolve rate
metrics.description: The share of repository tasks whose applied patch passes the fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests. This is the SWE-bench resolved rate, adapted to the client's own issues when they have a repo, a patch, and tests. It is stricter than code_tests_pass on a single function because the patch must apply and must not break existing tests.
metrics.measures: Whether a code change resolves a task inside a real repository.

signals: The model emits a diff or edits files
The repo has a test suite that failed before the change
You can run the suite in a sandbox

when_not_to_use: The task is a single self-contained function. code_tests_pass is enough and the patch machinery adds failure modes.
You cannot apply the patch cleanly because the base revision is not pinned. Fix the harness before comparing models.

required_inputs.notes: Pin the base commit. Separate harness failures (patch did not apply, dependency install failed) from test failures.

computation.formula: resolve_rate = tasks where fail-to-pass tests now pass and pass-to-pass tests still pass / tasks.
procedure: Apply the patch to the pinned base.
Run fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests.
Mark the task resolved only if both groups succeed. Report apply failures separately.

interpretation.meaning: Every task's patch applied and the test split passed.
A number that has been a serious result on public repo benchmarks. Compare against the client's own base rate, not against a leaderboard screenshot.
No task was resolved.

cost_effort.notes: The most expensive code metric here. Use a subset for iteration and the full set for the decision.

limitations: Weak tests let a bad patch count as resolved. Prefer a verified subset when you have one.
Harness failures counted as model failures will rank the patch format rather than the fix.

metrics.name: Syntax-valid rate
metrics.description: The share of outputs that parse in the target language. It is a floor, not functional correctness. A program can parse and still be wrong. Use it as a gate beside tests, or as the only code metric when tests do not exist yet.
metrics.measures: Whether the candidate is syntactically valid code in the declared language.

use_cases: early evals before tests are written
signals: The output is code or a config with a parser
You see markdown fences and prose mixed into code
Tests are slow and you want a fast pre-check

when_not_to_use: Tests exist. Syntax validity is implied by a passing run often enough that it should not also sit in Q. Keep it as a diagnostic or a gate.
The language has no parser you can pin. A regex is not a syntax check.

required_inputs.notes: Config language selects the parser. Strip a single markdown fence before parsing and record that you did.

computation.formula: syntax_valid_rate = parseable_outputs / outputs.
procedure: Extract the code span.
Parse with the pinned compiler or parser. Do not execute.
Average. Report the dominant parse error.
implementations: JSON and YAML parsers for those formats

interpretation.meaning: Every output parsed.
A reasonable floor. The remaining failures are usually fences, prose, or truncation.
Nothing parsed.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 when unparseable output breaks a pipeline.

cost_effort.notes: Very cheap. Do not pay a judge to check syntax.

limitations: Parse success is not behavioral correctness.
Template languages and DSLs need their own parser. Do not silently use Python's.

metrics.name: Conversation completeness
metrics.description: Whether the dialogue achieved the user's goal by the end: the question was answered, the task was done, or the correct next step was reached. This is outcome-level and should lead the quality score for support chats when a goal can be defined. Turn-level metrics do not capture a bot that is polite and unfinished.
metrics.measures: Goal completion over a full conversation.

signals: A conversation has a goal you can label
Success is a property of the whole transcript, not one turn
You have historical chats with resolution labels, or you can write goal checks

when_not_to_use: There is no defined goal. A judge asked if the chat feels complete will invent one. Use turn_relevancy until goals exist.
Completion is fully determined by tool state. agent_task_success on the final state is tighter.

required_inputs.notes: Prefer a human or rule label of success. A judge is acceptable when the goal statement is written on the case.

computation.formula: completeness = conversations whose goal is met / conversations.
procedure: Attach a goal statement or success label to each dialogue.
Decide met or not met from the full transcript and any tool state.
Average. Break out abandonment separately when the user simply left.
implementations: τ-bench task success is the tool-using cousin agent_task_success

interpretation.meaning: Every dialogue reached its goal.
Most dialogues finish. Read the unfinished goals by type.
No dialogue reached its goal.

cost_effort.driver: One judgment per conversation, unless the label is already in the logs.
cost_effort.notes: If production already labels resolution, this metric is a join, not a judge call.

limitations: A goal can be met with a rude or ungrounded answer. Keep risk and grounding metrics.
User simulators used to generate the other side become part of the score. Pin the simulator.

metrics.name: Knowledge retention
metrics.description: Whether later turns still respect facts the user stated earlier, such as a plan, a name, a constraint, or a correction. DeepEval's knowledge retention metric is this construct. Forgetting a correction mid-chat is a common support failure.
metrics.measures: Recall and consistency of user-provided facts across the dialogue.

use_cases: any assistant that collects details over turns
signals: Users state facts in early turns that later answers must use
Transcripts show the bot contradicting an earlier correction
The dialogue is multi-turn

when_not_to_use: The conversation is a single turn. There is nothing to retain.
The facts to retain are in a document, not in the user's earlier turns. That is faithfulness.

required_inputs.notes: The judge extracts user facts from earlier turns and checks later assistant turns. A human can supply the fact list instead.

computation.formula: retention = user_facts that later assistant turns still respect / user_facts introduced.
procedure: List facts the user introduced or corrected.
Check each later assistant reference to that fact.
Score the fraction still respected. A contradiction fails the fact.

interpretation.meaning: Later turns respected every user-provided fact.
Most facts stuck. The misses are usually corrections the model overwrote.
No user fact was retained, or every one was contradicted.

cost_effort.driver: A judge pass over the transcript.
cost_effort.notes: One call per conversation is usually enough if the transcript fits the judge context.

limitations: The metric misses facts the extractor drops. On high-stakes chats, supply the fact list.
A model can avoid contradiction by never using the fact. Count a required use as a miss if the task needed it.

metrics.name: Multi-turn coherence
metrics.description: Whether the assistant's turns form a consistent dialogue: it does not contradict itself, drop the thread, or restart the conversation without reason. This is discourse coherence across turns, distinct from knowledge_retention, which is specifically about user-provided facts.
metrics.measures: Internal consistency and thread continuity of the assistant across a dialogue.

signals: Conversations run past a handful of turns
Logs show the bot contradicting its own earlier answer
You are comparing models that otherwise tie on single-turn quality

when_not_to_use: Dialogues are two turns. The metric has little to see.
The contradiction is with a source document. Use faithfulness or contradiction_rate.

required_inputs.notes: Judge the assistant's own consistency. User contradictions are not the assistant's score.

computation.formula: A 0–1 rubric: 1 if the assistant never contradicts itself and the thread is continuous, otherwise a judge score equal to consistent_turns / assistant_turns.
procedure: Read the assistant turns in order.
Mark self-contradictions and dropped threads.
Score the fraction of turns that remain consistent with earlier assistant commitments.
implementations: MT-Bench multi-turn judgments, narrowed to consistency

interpretation.meaning: The assistant stayed consistent across the dialogue.
Half the turns fight earlier turns or drop the thread.
The dialogue does not hold together.

cost_effort.notes: Skip on short chats. The failures show up later in the conversation.

limitations: A model can be coherently wrong. Coherence is not accuracy.
Judges under-detect numeric contradictions across distant turns.

metrics.name: Role adherence
metrics.description: The share of assistant turns that stay inside the assigned role and refuse to take on a different one. Support bots that become general assistants, or that break a persona the brand requires, fail this. DeepEval's role adherence and role-violation metrics are the same construct from opposite directions.
metrics.measures: Whether the assistant remains the role the system prompt defined.

use_cases: characters with a written role card
signals: A system prompt defines a role and forbids others
Users try to pull the bot off role
Brand or clinical policy depends on the role boundary

when_not_to_use: There is no written role. Do not infer one from the product name.
The behavior you care about is harm, not persona. Use safety_violation. A villain role is not a reason to allow harm.

required_inputs.notes: The role card is the policy_spec. Include out-of-role user probes in the set if that is the production failure.

computation.formula: role_adherence = in_role_assistant_turns / assistant_turns.
procedure: Score each assistant turn against the role card.
Count a turn that adopts a forbidden role as a miss.
Average within conversations, then across them.
implementations: DeepEval RoleViolationMetric as 1 minus this rate

interpretation.meaning: Every turn stayed in role.
A typical bar for a branded assistant before you consider a gate.
No turn stayed in role.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.98 when leaving the role creates legal or clinical risk.

cost_effort.driver: One judgment per turn or per conversation.
cost_effort.notes: Batch turns into one judge call when the transcript fits.

limitations: Role cards that contradict safety policy must not win. Safety gates override role.
Judges are literal. A permitted escalation to a human can look like breaking character unless the card allows it.

metrics.name: Topic adherence
metrics.description: The share of assistant turns that stay on the allowed topics and do not follow the user into out-of-scope subjects. Ragas topic adherence and DeepEval's topic metric measure this. It is how a bank's card bot stays a card bot.
metrics.measures: Whether the assistant remains within a configured topic allow-list.

use_cases: public-sector assistants with a defined scope
signals: The product has an allow-list of topics
Out-of-scope requests are common in logs
Leaving the topic creates liability even when the answer would be fine elsewhere

when_not_to_use: The assistant is a general chatbot. Topic adherence would punish its job.
The harm is the content, not the subject. A toxic answer on an allowed topic needs toxicity_rate or safety_violation.

required_inputs.notes: policy_spec is the allow-list and the refusal behavior you want when the user leaves it. Refusing an off-topic request counts as adherence.

computation.formula: topic_adherence = on_topic_assistant_turns / assistant_turns. A correct refusal of an off-topic request is on topic.
procedure: Label each assistant turn against the allow-list.
Count a helpful off-topic answer as a miss.
Average. Report the off-topic topics that slipped through.

interpretation.meaning: Every turn stayed in scope or refused cleanly.
Mostly in scope. Review the leaks.
The assistant did not stay on the allow-list.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.95 for narrow regulated assistants.

cost_effort.driver: A judge with the allow-list in prompt.
cost_effort.notes: Similar to role adherence. Do not run both unless role and topic actually differ in the policy.

limitations: Allow-lists are ambiguous at the edges. Write borderline examples into the spec.
A model that refuses everything scores well. Pair with over_refusal or conversation_completeness.

metrics.name: Turn relevancy
metrics.description: The share of assistant turns that address the user's latest request given the dialogue so far. This is the multi-turn form of answer relevancy. A single off-topic turn can fail a support conversation even if the closing summary is fine.
metrics.measures: Whether each assistant turn responds to the user turn it follows.

signals: The transcript has more than one user turn
The product is a conversation rather than a single completion
Users complain that the bot answers a different question

when_not_to_use: The task is single-turn. Use answer_relevancy. Scoring turns on a one-shot prompt adds nothing.
The assistant is supposed to redirect off-topic users. A strict relevancy judge will punish the redirect unless the rubric allows it.

required_inputs.notes: Score assistant turns only. Provide the role policy if redirection is allowed.

computation.formula: turn_relevancy = relevant_assistant_turns / assistant_turns.
procedure: Walk assistant turns in order.
Judge each one against the dialogue prefix.
Average within the conversation, then across conversations.

interpretation.meaning: Every assistant turn addressed the dialogue.
One weak turn in five. Read those turns before weighting the metric heavily.
No assistant turn was relevant.

score.aggregation: Macro-average over conversations so a long chat does not dominate.

cost_effort.notes: Cost grows with turns. Sample long transcripts if needed and record the sampling.

limitations: Judges confuse politeness with relevance.
A turn can be relevant and still wrong. Pair with faithfulness or a task metric.

metrics.name: Cache hit rate
metrics.description: Cached input tokens divided by prompt tokens, from provider usage. Higher means more of the prompt was billed at the cache price. Report it for RAG and agents with a repeated prefix. It is not quality.
metrics.measures: The fraction of the prompt served from the provider's prompt cache.

use_cases: RAG with a stable system prompt
agents with a repeated tool preamble
signals: The provider exposes cached token counts
Prompts share a long prefix
Cache pricing is materially lower

when_not_to_use: The provider does not report cached tokens. A client-side guess is not this metric.
As a quality term. Caching does not make answers better.

required_inputs.notes: Use the provider's cached-token field. Do not infer hits from latency.

computation.formula: cache_hit_rate = cached_prompt_tokens / prompt_tokens.
procedure: Sum cached and prompt tokens.
Divide.
Apply the cache price inside cost_per_case_usd so the rate and the dollars agree.

interpretation.meaning: Most of the prompt was cached. Input price is close to the cache price.
No cached tokens. You paid full input price, or the provider did not report cache.

score.aggregation: Pooled tokens, not the mean of per-call rates, so short calls do not dominate.

cost_effort.notes: Free when the field exists.

limitations: A high hit rate can mean the benchmark reused prefixes the production mix will not. Match the production prefix distribution.
Providers count cache eligibility differently.

metrics.name: Cost per case
metrics.description: The provider-billed dollar cost of one case, from reported token usage and the price snapshot: uncached input, cached input, and output, including reasoning tokens if the provider bills them. This is the catalogue metric cost_per_case_usd. It is always measured. Ranking uses cost per success, which divides by the pass rate.
metrics.measures: Dollars spent to produce one case, successful or not.

use_cases: the cost axis before quality filtering
signals: The run calls a priced endpoint
Usage is on the response
A price table exists for the provider

when_not_to_use: As the only cost number on the recommendation card. A cheap model that rarely succeeds is not cheap. Lead with cost_per_success_usd and keep this beside it.
Self-hosted GPUs with no token invoice. Use self_host_cost_per_mtok.

required_inputs.notes: Prices are USD per token. Stamp the price snapshot date. Catalogue id cost_per_case_usd. Cached tokens are priced at the cache rate, not the full input rate.

computation.formula: cost = (prompt_tokens - cached_tokens) * p_in + cached_tokens * p_cache + completion_tokens * p_out. Reasoning tokens are included in whichever bucket the provider bills.
procedure: Read provider usage, including cache and reasoning fields.
Apply the pinned price snapshot.
Average per case. Do not use a blended price that hides cache.

interpretation.meaning: A tenth of a cent per case. Meaningful only against the client's volume and quality.
Five cents per case. Material at high volume, irrelevant for a rare internal tool.

score.aggregation: Mean USD per case, plus the total.

cost_effort.notes: Always on. The measurement is free. The spend is the run itself.

limitations: List price is not the invoice if the contract has discounts. Use contract prices when the client has them.
A local tokenizer estimate will not match the bill. Prefer provider usage.

metrics.name: Cost per successful case
metrics.description: Total spend divided by the number of cases that passed the quality checks and the gates. This is the catalogue metric cost_per_success_usd and the cost number used for ranking. It charges the model for failures, retries, and judge-free waste. Lower is better.
metrics.measures: Dollars per case that actually succeeded.

use_cases: comparing a cheap weak model with an expensive strong one
signals: Every run
Quality metrics define a pass bit
The architecture says to rank on cost per successful case

when_not_to_use: No quality metric is defined, so every completion counts as success. Then this equals cost per case and you should say so.
Success is so rare that the denominator is a handful of cases. The point estimate is wild. Report the interval.

required_inputs.notes: The pass bit comes from the selected quality metrics and gates, not from HTTP success. Catalogue id cost_per_success_usd.

computation.formula: cost_per_success = sum(cost) / max(n_success, 1), and undefined if n_success is 0. Report undefined rather than infinity in the UI, and do not rank an all-fail model as costly in a way that hides the failure.
procedure: Sum cost across all attempts, including failures.
Count cases that passed quality and gates.
Divide. If the count is zero, mark the candidate as having no successes.

interpretation.meaning: Everything succeeded. The two numbers meeting is a good sign.

interpretation.at: much larger than cost per case
interpretation.meaning: Most of the spend bought failures.

cost_effort.notes: Always on once a pass bit exists.

limitations: The pass bit's definition changes the cost. Stamp which metrics were required to pass.
Judge costs are real money too. Include them if the client pays them, and label them separately.

metrics.name: Projected monthly cost
metrics.description: Cost per case times the client's monthly call volume. This is the catalogue metric monthly_cost_usd. It is the number on the recommendation card, not a measured invoice. It is undefined without a volume.
metrics.measures: A projection of monthly spend from per-case cost and stated volume.

signals: The user entered a monthly volume
You are translating per-case cost into a budget

when_not_to_use: Volume is unknown. Leave the projection blank rather than inventing a volume.
As a measured result. It is a multiplication.

required_inputs.notes: Volume is a user input. Catalogue id monthly_cost_usd. State whether the per-case term is cost per case or cost per success.

computation.formula: monthly = cost_per_case * monthly_volume. The card may also show cost_per_success * volume. Label which.
procedure: Take the measured per-case cost.
Multiply by the entered volume.
Show the arithmetic. Do not present the product as an invoice.

interpretation.meaning: The savings line on the card. It is only as good as the volume and the pass rate.
No volume was entered. Omit the dollar savings.

cost_effort.notes: Free. The sensitive input is the volume, which is the client's.

limitations: Volume is often a guess. Say so.
The projection ignores retries, judge cost, and failed calls unless you used cost per success.

metrics.name: Reasoning-token ratio
metrics.description: Reasoning tokens divided by all output tokens. Report-only. It shows whether a reasoning mode is buying accuracy with a large hidden trace. Compare reasoning-effort settings as separate candidates rather than averaging them.
metrics.measures: What fraction of the output bill is the reasoning trace.

signals: Candidates have a reasoning mode
Usage splits reasoning tokens

when_not_to_use: The provider does not report the split. Do not estimate it from the visible answer length.
As a quality score. A long trace can be waste or it can be the work.

required_inputs.notes: Requires a reasoning token field on usage.

computation.formula: ratio = reasoning_tokens / max(completion_tokens, 1), under the provider's definition of those fields.
procedure: Read the split.
Divide.
Report the mean ratio next to accuracy so effort levels can be judged.

interpretation.meaning: Most of the output bill is the trace, not the answer.
No reasoning tokens were billed, or the mode was off.

cost_effort.notes: Free when the provider reports the split.

limitations: Providers define reasoning tokens differently.
A low ratio is not efficiency if the answer is wrong.

metrics.name: Self-hosted cost per million tokens
metrics.description: An estimate of dollars per million tokens for a deployment the client would run: GPU hourly price times GPU count, divided by goodput, adjusted for utilization. It exists so a token API can be compared with owning the GPUs. It is an estimate with a dated price snapshot, not an invoice.
metrics.measures: Estimated self-hosted unit cost at a stated goodput and utilization.

signals: The client asked about self-hosting
GPU price and a goodput measurement exist

when_not_to_use: You have no goodput measurement. Dividing a GPU price by a hoped-for token rate is not this metric.
As a precise TCO. Power, networking, and people are outside the formula. Say so.

required_inputs.notes: GPU prices are a dated snapshot. goodput comes from goodput_rps converted to tokens with the measured tokens per request.

computation.formula: usd_per_mtok = gpu_usd_per_hour * gpu_count / (tokens_per_hour_at_goodput * utilization) * 1e6.
procedure: Measure goodput on the hardware you are pricing.
Multiply GPU price by count.
Divide. Stamp the GPU price date and the utilization assumption.
implementations: The self-host formula in the BIY metrics research note

interpretation.meaning: The GPU estimate is cheaper at the stated utilization. It still omits operations labor.
The API is cheaper at this utilization. Self-hosting may still win for data-residency reasons that are not in the formula.

score.aggregation: One estimate per hardware and utilization assumption.

cost_effort.driver: A goodput run on the hardware.
cost_effort.notes: Not part of the default API benchmark. Add it when self-hosting is actually a candidate.

limitations: Utilization is an assumption. A low real utilization destroys the estimate.
GPU spot prices move. The research note treats them as dated snapshots for that reason.
provenance: BIY research note on self-host cost

metrics.name: Input tokens per case
metrics.description: Mean input tokens per case from provider usage. Report-only. It explains why two models with the same price per token cost different amounts on the same text, and it is the denominator behind cache savings.
metrics.measures: Billed prompt size in provider tokens, including any billed tool schema.

use_cases: checking that candidates saw the same prompt
signals: Every run
Prompts are long or include retrieved context

when_not_to_use: As a quality or speed score.
As proof that the prompts were identical. Different tokenizers bill different counts for the same string. Compare the string, not only the count.

required_inputs.notes: Provider prompt token count, including any tool schema the provider billed.

computation.formula: mean prompt tokens per case.
procedure: Read prompt usage.
Average.
If candidates differ by more than tokenization can explain, the prompts were not the same. Stop the comparison.

interpretation.meaning: The comparison is fair at the prompt layer, up to tokenizer differences.
Check tool schemas and chat templates. Something extra is being billed.

cost_effort.notes: Negligible next to the model call. No judge and no extra request.

limitations: Tokenizer inequality is real. A higher count is not automatically a worse prompt.
Cached and uncached input should also be split. See cache_hit_rate.

metrics.name: Output tokens per case
metrics.description: Mean output tokens per case, split into reasoning tokens and answer tokens when the provider reports the split. This is the catalogue metric tokens_out_per_case. It explains cost and latency. A model with a low token price and a long hidden trace can still be the expensive one.
metrics.measures: How much the model emits, including hidden reasoning.

signals: Every priced run
Reasoning models are in the candidate set

when_not_to_use: As a quality metric. Shorter is not better. Verbosity bias in judges is a reason to report length, not to reward it.
Across tokenizers as a measure of information. It is a billing quantity.

required_inputs.notes: Use provider completion and reasoning counts. Catalogue id tokens_out_per_case.

computation.formula: mean completion tokens per case, with reasoning tokens broken out when present.
procedure: Read usage on each call.
Average.
Split reasoning and answer. Do not rank models by this column.

interpretation.meaning: The trace, not the answer, is the bill. Compare reasoning-effort settings as separate candidates.
Look at truncation_rate. The model is hitting the ceiling.

score.aggregation: Mean and p95 of output tokens.

cost_effort.notes: Always on. It explains the cost axis.

limitations: Token counts are tokenizer-specific.
Some providers fold reasoning into completion without a split. Say when the split is missing.

metrics.name: Cold-start latency
metrics.description: Time from a scale-to-zero or first-use state until the first successful completion. Lower is better. It matters for sporadic internal tools and serverless endpoints, and it should not be mixed into the steady-state TTFT.
metrics.measures: Latency of the first success after an idle or cold state.

signals: The endpoint scales to zero
Traffic is bursty with long gaps
The first user after idle has a different SLO

when_not_to_use: The endpoint is warm and kept that way. Cold start is not in the user's experience. Do not average it into TTFT.
You cannot actually cool the endpoint. A guessed cold start is not a measurement.

required_inputs.notes: The harness waits until the provider reports idle or uses a fresh deployment, then times the first success.

computation.formula: cold_start_ms = t_first_success - t_cold_request.
procedure: Confirm the endpoint is cold.
Send one request and time the first success.
Report it separately from steady-state percentiles.
implementations: A single discarded warmup, reported rather than discarded

interpretation.meaning: A short cold start that many interactive flows can hide.
A long cold start. Fine only if the product warms the endpoint or is not interactive.

score.aggregation: Median over a handful of cold trials. One trial is an anecdote.

cost_effort.driver: Idle time and repeated cold trials.
cost_effort.notes: Not part of the default run. Add it only for scale-to-zero endpoints.

limitations: Providers change idle policy. Stamp the date.
A cold start that includes model download is a different number from a paused replica. Say which you measured.
provenance: BIY research notes on cold start

metrics.name: End-to-end latency
metrics.description: Milliseconds from request send to the final token. This is the catalogue metric e2e_ms. It is the speed metric for synchronous extraction and classification, where the caller cannot use a partial result. Report p50, p95, and p99.
metrics.measures: Full wait from request send until the response is complete.

signals: The caller waits for the full payload
The kind is extraction or classification
A p95 latency target is in the profile

when_not_to_use: The user reads a stream and the first token is what they feel. Lead with ttft_ms. E2E still describes the total but should not be the only speed number.
The work is an asynchronous batch. Per-call e2e is not the capacity metric. Use throughput_rps or goodput_rps.

required_inputs.notes: t_last is the final chunk. Exclude errors from the distribution. Catalogue id e2e_ms.

computation.formula: e2e_ms = t_last - t0.
procedure: Timestamp send and final chunk.
Compute percentiles on successes.
The extraction and classification speed scores use p95.

interpretation.meaning: A one-second full response. Fine for many internal tools, tight for some interactive forms.
Five seconds. Often past a synchronous request budget.

score.suggested_gate: p95 <= the profile maximum for synchronous calls.

cost_effort.notes: Free on the quality run. Streaming timestamps are already recorded.

limitations: E2E grows with output length. A more verbose model looks slower. Report tokens as well.
Retries inside the client inflate e2e. Time the attempt you score, and count retries in reliability.

metrics.name: Goodput
metrics.description: The request rate you can sustain while TTFT and inter-token latency stay inside their SLOs at a high percentile. It is the capacity number that does not trade away the latency budget. Higher is better. Use it when the client has both a latency SLO and a volume target.
metrics.measures: Throughput that still meets the latency SLOs.

use_cases: batch that still has a freshness SLO
signals: There is a TTFT or ITL SLO
Volume is high enough that concurrency will push latency
A raw throughput number has been used to justify a stack that misses the SLO

when_not_to_use: There is no latency SLO. throughput_rps is the simpler capacity number.
You cannot run a concurrency sweep. A single concurrency does not identify the maximum goodput.

required_inputs.notes: SLOs are config: for example TTFT p99 and ITL p99. The sweep is a separate run from the quality benchmark.

computation.formula: goodput = max request rate such that the configured latency SLOs hold.
procedure: Sweep concurrency.
At each level, measure throughput and the latency percentiles.
Take the highest throughput whose percentiles meet the SLOs.
implementations: Goodput as described in serving guides from vLLM and NIM-style SLOs

interpretation.meaning: The useful capacity. Higher raw throughput above this point is not free.
Even the lowest tested rate missed the SLO.

cost_effort.notes: A sizing exercise, not part of every model comparison. Skip it for the default recommendation run.

limitations: The SLOs define the number. Publish them.
A short sweep mis-locates the boundary.

metrics.name: Inter-token latency
metrics.description: The mean gap between successive output tokens after the first, in milliseconds. Also called TPOT. It is the smoothness of the stream. A snappy TTFT with a stuttering stream still feels broken for long answers.
metrics.measures: Average per-token delay during generation.

use_cases: SLOs that constrain both TTFT and ITL
signals: Answers are long
Users read the stream
You are defining a goodput SLO

when_not_to_use: Outputs are a few tokens, such as a label. ITL is noise. Use e2e_ms.
You cannot see per-token timestamps, only a full response. Do not invent ITL from e2e and a token count if the server batched the whole answer.

required_inputs.notes: Compute from token timestamps when you have them. Otherwise (t_last - t_first) / max(output_tokens - 1, 1) on a stream that sent incremental tokens.

computation.formula: ITL = (t_last - t_first) / max(n_output_tokens - 1, 1).
procedure: Measure the generation interval after the first token.
Divide by the number of following tokens, not chunks.
Report p50 and p95 of per-request ITL.
implementations: Anyscale and NVIDIA NIM ITL / TPOT
Artificial Analysis output speed is the reciprocal view

interpretation.meaning: About 50 tokens per second. Comfortable for reading in English.
About 10 tokens per second. A stream that feels stuck for a long answer.

score.aggregation: p50 and p95 of per-request mean ITL.

cost_effort.notes: Free on a real stream.

limitations: Chunking makes a naive per-chunk latency meaningless. Divide by tokens.
Reasoning tokens inflate or deflate ITL depending on whether they are in the numerator. State the choice.

metrics.name: Output tokens per second
metrics.description: Output tokens after the first, divided by the generation interval. This is the catalogue metric output_tps and the reciprocal of ITL. The product table uses it with TTFT for user-facing chat. Higher is better.
metrics.measures: Decode speed once generation has started.

use_cases: comparing fast variants of the same weights
signals: The user reads a stream
Answers are longer than a sentence
The kind is chat

when_not_to_use: You would also put ITL into the speed score. They are reciprocals. Pick output_tps for the speed axis and keep ITL as a diagnostic if an SLO is written in milliseconds.
The entire response arrives in one chunk. You do not have a decode rate.

required_inputs.notes: Catalogue id output_tps. Count tokens with the provider's usage when available, not with a local tokenizer, so the rate matches billing.

computation.formula: output_tps = max(n_output_tokens - 1, 0) / ((t_last - t_first) / 1000).
procedure: Measure the interval after the first token.
Divide the remaining output tokens by seconds.
Report median tokens per second. Do not average speeds across calls with a mean of ratios if you can report a pooled rate. Say which you did.

interpretation.meaning: A comfortable English reading pace.
A slow stream for a long answer.

score.aggregation: Median per-call rate, and a pooled rate.

cost_effort.notes: Free on the streamed run.

limitations: Tokenizer differences make tokens per second a poor comparison of information rate. Prefer it for the same model across providers, and pair it with time-to-done for users.
A high rate on tiny outputs is noise.

metrics.name: Task end-to-end time
metrics.description: Wall-clock milliseconds for a multi-step agent task, including tool time and every model call. This is the catalogue metric task_e2e_ms and the speed metric for agents. A fast model that takes twenty steps can lose to a slower model that finishes in three.
metrics.measures: Wall-clock duration of a multi-step task, including tool calls.

use_cases: anything the user waits on as a task rather than a token
signals: The kind is agent
A task has several model calls or tools
The profile scores agent speed as end-to-end per task

when_not_to_use: The task is a single call. e2e_ms is the same number and the clearer name.
Tool latency dominates and varies in the sandbox. Attribute model time and tool time or you will rank the sandbox.

required_inputs.notes: Start at the user task and stop at the final answer or the step cap. Catalogue id task_e2e_ms.

computation.formula: task_e2e_ms = t_task_end - t_task_start, including tool time unless config excludes it.
procedure: Clock the episode.
Split model time and tool time.
Report p50 and p95 of task time. The agent speed score uses this, not TTFT.

interpretation.meaning: A five-second task. Plausible for a short tool flow.
A one-minute task. Interactive users have usually left.

score.suggested_gate: p95 <= the profile maximum for interactive agents.

cost_effort.notes: Free if the harness logs start and end.

limitations: Tool latency can dominate. Publish the split.
Failed tasks that hit the step cap look slow. Report them with pass_hat_k, not as a latency win when you drop them.

metrics.name: Throughput
metrics.description: Completed requests per second at a stated concurrency. This is the catalogue metric throughput_rps. It is a capacity metric for batch and for sizing, not the latency a single user feels. Higher is better. The catalogue marks a full concurrency sweep as a stretch goal.
metrics.measures: Sustained completed requests per second.

use_cases: comparing deployments of the same model
signals: The workload is batch or high volume
You can run at a controlled concurrency
Someone asks how many calls per second the deployment sustains

when_not_to_use: You only have single-call latencies. Do not invert e2e and call it throughput. Throughput needs concurrent load.
As the chat speed score. A high-throughput endpoint can have a poor p95 TTFT.

required_inputs.notes: Config concurrency is part of the result. Catalogue id throughput_rps. Throttled calls are counted in throttle_rate and are not successes.

computation.formula: throughput_rps = successful_completions / wall_seconds at concurrency N.
procedure: Run a fixed concurrency for a warmup plus a measurement window.
Count successes over the window.
Publish N with the number. A throughput without concurrency is meaningless.

interpretation.meaning: Read it only against another candidate at the same concurrency, prompt length, and success definition.
Nothing completed in the window.

cost_effort.notes: Do not add this to every quality run. It is a separate capacity test.

limitations: The rate depends on prompt length, concurrency, and what you do with failures.
Provider rate limits cap the measurement. throttle_rate tells you when that happened.

metrics.name: Time to first answer token
metrics.description: Milliseconds from request send to the first answer token, skipping reasoning tokens. This is the catalogue metric ttfat_ms. Use it when the UI hides the reasoning trace, because TTFT then measures a wait the user does not see as an answer.
metrics.measures: Delay until the first visible answer token, excluding hidden reasoning.

use_cases: UIs that collapse the reasoning trace
signals: Candidates include reasoning models
The UI does not show the reasoning trace
TTFT looks unfairly bad for models that think first

when_not_to_use: The product shows reasoning tokens as they stream. TTFT is the user-visible wait.
The provider does not separate reasoning and answer deltas. Do not guess. Fall back to TTFT and say so.

required_inputs.notes: Requires the stream to mark reasoning versus answer channels, or an equivalent provider field. Catalogue id ttfat_ms.

computation.formula: ttfat_ms = t_first_answer - t0.
procedure: Identify the first answer-channel delta.
Subtract t0.
Report p50 and p95 next to TTFT so the reasoning overhead is visible.
implementations: Artificial Analysis time to first answer token

interpretation.meaning: A plausible chat target when a short hidden trace is acceptable. The profile decides.
A long silent wait before the answer. Poor for interactive chat.

score.suggested_gate: p95 <= the profile maximum when reasoning is hidden.

cost_effort.notes: Free on a stream that distinguishes reasoning from the answer.

limitations: Providers differ on whether reasoning deltas are marked. An unmarked trace makes this metric equal to a guess. Skip it.
A fast first answer token can still be a slow full answer. Read output_tps and e2e_ms.

metrics.name: Time to first token
metrics.description: Milliseconds from the request being sent to the first non-empty token, including network, queueing, and prefill. This is the catalogue metric ttft_ms and the speed metric for user-facing chat. Report p50 and p95. The p95 is what the product table uses for chat.
metrics.measures: How long a person waits before anything starts appearing.

use_cases: any UI that shows tokens as they arrive
signals: The handler streams to a user who is waiting
The kind is chat
A TTFT target is in the trade-off profile

when_not_to_use: The job is a batch with no one waiting. TTFT does not belong in the speed score. Cost does.
The model emits a long hidden reasoning trace before the answer and the UI hides reasoning. ttfat_ms is the wait the user feels. Still record TTFT.

required_inputs.notes: t0 is when the request is sent. t_first is the first non-empty content or reasoning delta. Streaming is required. Catalogue id ttft_ms.

computation.formula: ttft_ms = t_first - t0, in milliseconds. Report p50 and p95 across successful streamed calls.
procedure: Record t0 and the first content or reasoning delta on the stream.
Exclude failed calls from the latency distribution and count them in error_rate.
Publish p50 and p95. The chat speed score uses p95 against the profile target.

interpretation.meaning: A typical interactive target. The profile, not this bank, sets the client's target.
A wait that feels broken for chat. Often a maximum in the speed score.

score.aggregation: p50 and p95 of successful calls. Mean is not the headline.
score.suggested_gate: p95 <= the profile maximum for user-facing chat.

cost_effort.driver: Timestamps on calls you already make.
cost_effort.notes: Free if you stream. Do not run a separate latency benchmark with a different prompt length.

limitations: TTFT scales with prompt length. Compare models at the client's length distribution.
Reasoning tokens count as the first token. A reasoning model can look slow on TTFT and fast on time to the visible answer. Report ttfat_ms too when reasoning is hidden.

metrics.name: Constraint satisfaction rate
metrics.description: The fraction of individual constraints that pass, across all prompts. IFEval calls this instruction-level accuracy. A prompt with eight constraints and one miss scores 1 on this rate's micro form for the seven that passed, and 0 on strict prompt accuracy. Use the micro rate to see which constraint families fail.
metrics.measures: Per-constraint pass rate, not per-prompt all-or-nothing.

use_cases: debugging which rules a model misses
signals: Prompts bundle several constraints
Strict accuracy is hard to interpret because one rule dominates the failures
You want a quality term that gives partial credit

when_not_to_use: The product needs all constraints at once, such as a parser that rejects the whole payload. Gate on instruction_following and keep this as the breakdown.
As a second quality term beside strict accuracy. Put one in Q.

required_inputs.notes: Same verifiers as the strict metric. Config chooses micro over constraints or macro over constraint types.

computation.formula: micro = passed_constraints / constraints. Macro = unweighted mean of per-type pass rates.
procedure: Run every verifier.
Pool passes for the micro rate and group them by constraint type.
Publish both. Default Q uses micro only when partial credit is intended.

interpretation.meaning: Every constraint passed.
Nine in ten constraints hold. Strict prompt accuracy can be much lower.
No constraint passed.

score.aggregation: Micro over constraints, with a per-type table.

cost_effort.notes: Free if strict instruction following is already computed.

limitations: Micro averages let a model miss the one constraint you care about and still score well. Read the breakdown.
Constraints are not equally hard or important unless you weight them.

metrics.name: Instruction following (strict)
metrics.description: The share of prompts on which every verifiable constraint is satisfied, using the strict IFEval rule: the output must pass the checkers as written, without a second chance to strip a preamble. This is the catalogue metric instruction_following and the right score when the product depends on the constraints.
metrics.measures: Whether the whole output satisfies all of the prompt's checkable constraints at once.

use_cases: any prompt that says exactly, at most, or do not
signals: The system prompt contains checkable constraints
Downstream code or a brand review depends on those constraints
You can write a verifier rather than a vibe check

when_not_to_use: The only constraint is a JSON schema. json_schema_valid is the verifier. Do not also pay a judge to re-read the schema.
Constraints are subjective, such as 'sound friendly'. That is a rubric or tone_brand_fit, and it is not this metric.

required_inputs.notes: Verifiers are deterministic wherever possible: length, keyword, regex, JSON, case, language, bullet count. A judge is only for constraints that cannot be checked any other way, and those should be rare.

computation.formula: strict_prompt_accuracy = prompts where all constraints pass / prompts. This is IFEval's prompt-level strict accuracy.
procedure: Extract the constraint list from the prompt or from config.
Run each verifier on the raw output.
Pass the prompt only if every verifier passes. Also store constraint_satisfaction_rate.
implementations: IFEval strict prompt accuracy (Zhou et al., 2023)

interpretation.meaning: Every prompt passed every constraint on the raw output.
Most prompts fully comply. The failures are usually one constraint, which the micro rate will show.
No prompt satisfied all of its constraints.

score.aggregation: Mean over prompts. Publish the per-constraint breakdown.
score.suggested_gate: >= 0.95 when a violated constraint breaks downstream parsing or a legal requirement.

cost_effort.notes: Cheap if the constraints are verifiable. If you need a judge for most of them, you wrote the wrong checks.

limitations: Strict scoring fails a good answer that adds a short preamble. If the product allows that, use instruction_following_loose.
IFEval's public set is saturated by frontier models. Run the client's constraints, not the public set, for a recommendation.

metrics.name: Instruction following (loose)
metrics.description: IFEval's loose prompt accuracy. The same verifiers run on a small set of transformed outputs: raw, with the first line removed, with the last line removed, and with markdown fences stripped. A prompt passes if any transform passes. Use it when a wrapper around a correct payload is acceptable.
metrics.measures: Constraint satisfaction after the IFEval loose transforms.

use_cases: pipelines that strip a preamble before parsing
comparison with the strict score to see how much failure is formatting
signals: A thin wrapper around an otherwise correct answer is acceptable
You already report the strict score and want the loose companion
Failures are mostly fences or a one-line intro

when_not_to_use: The product consumes the raw string and a preamble would be shown to a user or a parser. Loose scoring hides a real defect. Use the strict metric.
As a second term in Q next to the strict score. They measure the same constraints. Pick one for Q and keep the other as a diagnostic.

required_inputs.notes: Uses the same verifiers as instruction_following. The transforms are part of the metric definition and should not grow into an open-ended repair loop.

computation.formula: loose_prompt_accuracy = prompts where any IFEval loose transform passes all verifiers / prompts.
procedure: Build the loose variants of the output.
Run the strict verifiers on each variant.
Pass the prompt if any variant fully passes.

interpretation.meaning: Every prompt passed under some allowed transform.
A large gap versus strict means the model is wrapping correct answers. Decide whether the wrapper matters before celebrating.
No transform satisfied the constraints.

cost_effort.driver: The same verifiers, a handful of times.
cost_effort.notes: Negligible incremental cost if the strict metric is already computed.

limitations: Loose transforms can accidentally delete the content a constraint was about, such as a required final line.
It is not a license to run an LLM 'fixer' before scoring.

metrics.name: Length within bounds
metrics.description: The output's length falls inside an inclusive minimum and maximum. This is the catalogue metric length_within. Use it whenever the UI, the SMS segment, or the prompt states a length bound. It is a gate, not a quality essay.
metrics.measures: Compliance with a character, token, word, or sentence bound.

signals: The prompt states a minimum or maximum length
The UI will truncate or reject out-of-range text
Tests assert a length

when_not_to_use: You want the summary to be short only if it still covers the source. summary_conciseness encodes that. A bare maximum does not.
The bound is in the model's max_tokens and truncation is the failure. truncation_rate already measures the API finish reason.

required_inputs.notes: Config min and max and the unit. Default unit is characters. Token bounds must name the tokenizer.

computation.formula: score = 1 if min <= length(output) <= max else 0. Either bound may be null.
procedure: Measure length in the configured unit.
Apply the inclusive bounds.
Average the passes. Also report the length distribution so a gate failure is explainable.

interpretation.meaning: Every output fell inside the bounds.
No output fell inside the bounds. Check whether the bound matches the unit.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 when the bound is a product constraint.

cost_effort.notes: Negligible next to the model call. No judge and no extra request.

limitations: Character length is not display length for emoji, CJK, or markup.
A model can satisfy the bound with filler or by deleting the answer.

metrics.name: Negative-constraint adherence
metrics.description: The share of 'do not' constraints that the output respects. Negative constraints fail differently from positive ones: models often do the banned thing because it was mentioned. When the ban is a known string, contains_none is the verifier. This metric covers bans that need a small checker or a judge, such as 'do not give a diagnosis'.
metrics.measures: Success at obeying prohibitions in the prompt.

use_cases: style bans that are not a word list
signals: The prompt contains explicit prohibitions
Failures in production are the model doing the banned thing
A word list is not sufficient

when_not_to_use: The ban is an enumerated phrase list. contains_none is deterministic. Use it.
The prohibition is a safety policy rather than a task instruction. Score safety_violation on an adversarial set, not only on the happy prompt.

required_inputs.notes: Prefer a deterministic checker. Use a judge only for semantic bans, and write the ban as a yes or no question.

computation.formula: adherence = respected_negative_constraints / negative_constraints.
procedure: List only the negative constraints.
Check each one. A violation fails that constraint.
Average. Do not mix positive constraints into this denominator.

interpretation.meaning: Every prohibition was respected.
A reasonable floor when the prohibition is user-visible.
Every prohibition was violated.

score.suggested_gate: >= 0.99 for bans that are also compliance requirements.

cost_effort.driver: Checkers, plus a judge only for semantic bans.
cost_effort.notes: Keep semantic bans few. Each one is a judge call.

limitations: Mentioning the ban in the judge prompt can bias the judge toward seeing a violation. Use a checklist.
A model can violate the spirit and pass a narrow checker. Review a sample.

metrics.name: G-Eval
metrics.description: A judge turns a natural-language criterion into evaluation steps, scores the output, and the score is the probability-weighted sum of the score tokens rather than the single sampled integer. This is the catalogue metric g_eval. It is the right instrument for a nuanced criterion such as summary coherence when a coarse rubric flickers between two adjacent scores.
metrics.measures: A criterion, scored with chain-of-thought steps and token probabilities.

use_cases: open-ended quality where 1–5 scores are unstable
signals: The criterion is nuanced and a single integer score flaps
The judge API returns token logprobs
You would otherwise have written a rubric with one vague criterion

when_not_to_use: Logprobs are unavailable. Fall back to rubric_score. Do not pretend a sampled integer is G-Eval.
You already have rubric_score on the same criteria. One instrument is enough.

required_inputs.notes: Pass the source document when the criterion is faithfulness-like or a summary. Config is the criterion text. Catalogue id g_eval. Without token logprobs this metric is not available. Use rubric_score.

computation.formula: p(s) = probability of the score token, renormalized over the allowed scores. raw = sum_s p(s) * s. stored = (raw - s_min) / (s_max - s_min).
procedure: Generate evaluation steps from the criterion once and freeze them.
Ask the judge to follow the steps and emit a score token.
Compute the probability-weighted score and normalize to 0–1.

interpretation.meaning: All score-token mass sat on the top score.
The probability mass is in the middle of the scale.
All mass sat on the bottom score.

cost_effort.driver: One judge call with logprobs per case, plus a one-time step generation.
cost_effort.notes: Similar price to a rubric, with a more stable number when logprobs exist.

limitations: Only the top token's probability is a crude approximation if the API does not return the alternatives. Require the full distribution over score tokens.
The method inherits judge biases. Steps help. They are not a human panel.

metrics.name: Length-controlled win rate
metrics.description: A pairwise win rate with the length difference regressed out, in the spirit of AlpacaEval's length-controlled win rate and LMSYS style control. Use it when candidates differ a lot in length and the uncorrected pairwise score tracks verbosity. It is a diagnostic correction, not a second quality construct.
metrics.measures: Preference against the baseline after accounting for length.

use_cases: open-ended generation where one model writes much more
checking that a pairwise win is not a length artifact
signals: pairwise_vs_baseline is selected
Output lengths differ substantially across candidates
You suspect verbosity bias

when_not_to_use: Lengths are similar. The correction adds noise. Report the plain pairwise rate.
As the only metric. It is still a judge preference. It does not become ground truth by controlling length.

required_inputs.notes: Built from the same pairwise judgments as pairwise_vs_baseline plus token lengths. A logistic regression with length difference as a covariate, following AlpacaEval LC. No extra judge call and no logprobs.

computation.formula: Fit a logistic model P(win) = sigmoid(a + b * length_gap) on the pairwise outcomes and report the predicted win rate at length_gap = 0. Range 0–1.
procedure: Reuse the both-order pairwise labels.
Record token lengths of both outputs.
Predict the win probability at zero length gap. Publish the uncorrected rate beside it.
implementations: LMSYS style control, of which length is one factor

interpretation.meaning: Parity with the baseline at equal length.

interpretation.at: far from the raw win rate
interpretation.meaning: The raw preference was largely a length effect. Trust this number more than the raw one.

score.aggregation: One regression per candidate against the frozen baseline.

cost_effort.driver: A regression on judgments you already paid for.
cost_effort.notes: Do not pay for a second judge. If pairwise judgments do not exist, do not select this.

limitations: Length is only one style factor. Markdown and lists also bias judges. LMSYS style control is broader. This metric only removes length.
The regression is unstable on small case counts. Prefer it above a few hundred pairs.

metrics.name: Pairwise win rate versus baseline
metrics.description: The rate at which a judge prefers the candidate's output to the baseline model's output on the same input, with the two orders averaged so a position bias becomes a tie. This is the catalogue metric pairwise_vs_baseline. Use it for open-ended quality when the question is 'is this as good as what we run today', not when an absolute rubric exists.
metrics.measures: Preference against the current production model on identical inputs.

use_cases: a migration off the incumbent model
signals: A baseline model can be run on the same cases
The output is open-ended
Stakeholders ask whether the new model is better than the current one

when_not_to_use: There is no baseline. A pairwise among only the candidates makes the score depend on who else showed up. HELM dropped that style of win rate for this reason. Use a rubric.
The task has a deterministic checker. Preference is a weaker instrument than tests, schemas, or exact fields.

required_inputs.notes: The baseline output is another model's completion on the same input, stored with the case. Both orders are required. Catalogue id pairwise_vs_baseline.

computation.formula: For each case, swap order. A disagreement is a tie. win_rate = (wins + 0.5 * ties) / cases. Range 0–1, with 0.5 meaning parity with the baseline.
procedure: Generate the baseline once and freeze it.
Judge both orders with a pinned judge from a different family than the candidates when possible.
Average. Report ties separately. Do not drop them.
implementations: LMSYS pairwise judging with order swap

interpretation.meaning: Parity with the baseline, including ties as half.
A modest preference for the candidate. Check that it survives order swapping and a length control.
The baseline is preferred. The candidate is behind the incumbent on this set.

score.aggregation: Mean over cases. This number is comparable across candidates because the baseline is fixed.

cost_effort.driver: A baseline generation plus two judge calls per case.
cost_effort.notes: The most expensive generic judge. Use it when the decision is a migration and a rubric feels untrustworthy.

limitations: Judges prefer longer, more formatted answers. See length_controlled_win_rate if lengths differ a lot.
A judge from the candidate's family tends to prefer that family. The architecture says to avoid that.

metrics.name: Rubric score
metrics.description: A judge scores the output against a rubric written for this use case, and the score is normalized to 0–1. This is the catalogue metric rubric_score and the default for open-ended work that has no tighter metric. The discovery agent drafts the rubric from the system prompt, with three to six criteria.
metrics.measures: The use case's own criteria, as a weighted rubric, not a generic notion of quality.

use_cases: generation with a written definition of good
anything without a reference or a schema
signals: No deterministic checker covers the quality you care about
